Improved dimension bounds for Falconer’s
distance problem in the plane

Alex Iosevich    Alexia Yavicoli
Abstract

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be analytic with t=dimHE>1t=\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1. We prove that its distance set satisfies dimHΔ​E≥45+η0\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E\geq\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0} for an absolute constant η0>0\eta_{0}>0, obtained by compactness without an explicit numerical value. We also obtain the explicit estimate

dimHΔ​E≥t2−2​t+52​t2−7​t+10for ​1<t≤11−414,\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E\geq\frac{t^{2}-2t+5}{2t^{2}-7t+10}\quad\text{for }1<t\leq\frac{11-\sqrt{41}}{4},

which reaches 78\frac{7}{8} at the right endpoint. For the pinned distance sets, we prove dimHΔx​E≥q∗=0.7813​…\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq q_{*}=0.7813\ldots for every x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} outside a set of Hausdorff dimension at most one, with stronger estimates depending on tt and further bounds on the exceptional sets. If EE is compact and supports an ss-Frostman measure μ\mu, where s>1s>1, then

dim¯B​Δx​E≥max⁡{45+η0,min⁡{3​s+15,78}}for μ-almost every ​x.\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}\Delta_{x}E\geq\max\left\{\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0},\min\left\{\frac{3s+1}{5},\frac{7}{8}\right\}\right\}\quad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x.

The same lower bound holds for pinned Hausdorff dimension under a common dyadic mass law, which may oscillate with the scale.

The proof retains information about both endpoints in the Kolmogorov complexity estimates of Stull and Fiedler–Stull. Applying the partition estimates with the roles of the endpoints reversed yields the bound 45\frac{4}{5} and the rational estimate above. To pass beyond 45\frac{4}{5}, we examine the constraints imposed by equality. Both information profiles must have excess information on a common interval of scales. Encoding a single source measure for all pins converts this constraint into a configuration of points and circles with many rich perpendicular bisectors. The lower bounds supplied by Katz–Tardos and Ren–Wang contradict the upper bound of Fu–Gan–Ren, forcing the fixed gain η0\eta_{0}. This passage from rigidity to a strict improvement has a precedent in the work of Héra, Shmerkin and Yavicoli on Furstenberg sets, where configurations close to the elementary bound are excluded using Bourgain’s projection theorem. A separate selection argument at each finite scale establishes the pinned lower box estimate for every ss-Frostman measure with s>1s>1.

Together with recent work of Stull, Fiedler, Csörnyei and their collaborators, these results illustrate how effective dimension and Kolmogorov complexity, in combination with Fourier analytic and combinatorial techniques, can yield new bounds in classical geometric measure theory.

1   Introduction

The Falconer distance problem is one of the most intriguing problems in modern geometric measure theory. Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, and define its distance set and its distance set pinned at x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, respectively, by

ΔE={|y−z|:y,z∈E},ΔxE={|x−y|:y∈E},\Delta E=\{|y-z|:y,z\in E\},\qquad\Delta_{x}E=\{|x-y|:y\in E\},

where |⋅||\cdot| denotes the Euclidean norm.

We call xx the pin and EE the source set. A source point is a point y∈Ey\in E from which the distance to the pin is measured. For x∈Ex\in E, Δx​E⊆Δ​E\Delta_{x}E\subseteq\Delta E.

For s≥0s\geq 0, define

ℋs(E)=limr↘0inf{∑i(diamUi)s:Ui⊆ℝ2,E⊆⋃iUi,diamUi≤r},\mathcal{H}^{s}(E)=\lim_{r\searrow 0}\inf\left\{\sum_{i}(\operatorname{diam}U_{i})^{s}:U_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2},\ E\subseteq\bigcup_{i}U_{i},\operatorname{diam}U_{i}\leq r\right\},

where the covers are countable and diam\operatorname{diam} denotes diameter. The Hausdorff dimension is dimHE=inf{s∈[0,∞):ℋs​(E)=0}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E=\inf\{s\in[0,\infty):\mathcal{H}^{s}(E)=0\}. The infimum in the display before taking the limit is the ss-dimensional Hausdorff content at scale rr. Omitting the restriction diam⁡Ui≤r\operatorname{diam}U_{i}\leq r defines the Hausdorff content without a scale restriction.

An analytic set is a continuous image of a complete separable metric space. Every Borel set is analytic. The question is how much of the size of EE must survive under the distance map. Falconer conjectured that Δ​E\Delta E has positive Lebesgue measure whenever dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1 [6]. Even the weaker conclusion dimHΔ​E=1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E=1 is open when dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E is only slightly larger than one.

For dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E slightly larger than one, the known lower bounds approach 34\frac{3}{4}. Stull [33, Theorem 1] proved that every analytic E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1 satisfies

dimH{x∈ℝ2:dimHΔx​E<12+dimHE4}≤1.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E<\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E}{4}\Bigr\}\leq 1.

Since this exceptional set cannot contain EE, also dimHΔ​E≥12+dimHE4\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E\geq\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E}{4}. Both bounds decrease to 34\frac{3}{4} as dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E decreases to one. We obtain improvements that remain positive in this limit.

Theorem 1.1 (A universal pinned bound).

Let α∗=10−3​e24−7​e=0.371107​…\alpha_{*}=\frac{10-3\mathrm{e}}{24-7\mathrm{e}}=0.371107\ldots, where e\mathrm{e} is the base of the natural logarithm, and

q∗=34+3​α∗40−12​α∗=0.78131​….q_{*}=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3\alpha_{*}}{40-12\alpha_{*}}=0.78131\ldots.

Every analytic E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1 satisfies

dimH{x∈ℝ2:dimHΔx​E<Q⁡(dimHE)}≤1,\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E<Q(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E)\right\}\leq 1,

where

Q⁡(t)=1−(1−q∗)​(3−2​t)1+(6−8​q∗)​(t−1)for ​1≤t≤32,Q(t)=1-\frac{(1-q_{*})(3-2t)}{1+(6-8q_{*})(t-1)}\quad\text{for }1\leq t\leq\frac{3}{2},

and Q⁡(t)=1Q(t)=1 for t≥32t\geq\frac{3}{2}. The function QQ is increasing on [1,32][1,\frac{3}{2}], with Q⁡(1)=q∗Q(1)=q_{*} and Q⁡(32)=1Q(\frac{3}{2})=1.

The exceptional set consists of the pins where the stated bound fails. We denote by B⁡(z,r)B(z,r) the open ball of radius rr about zz. A finite Borel measure ν\nu is ss-Frostman if ν⁡(B⁡(z,r))≤C​rs\nu(B(z,r))\leq Cr^{s} for every zz and 0<r≤10<r\leq 1, with CC independent of z,rz,r. Such a measure assigns mass zero to sets of Hausdorff dimension less than ss [23, Chapter 8]. Thus the conclusion holds for ν\nu-almost every pin whenever s>1s>1. The constant α∗\alpha_{*} comes from the estimate of Katz and Tardos for pairwise sums within rows of a matrix whose entries are all distinct [16, Corollary 5]. Katz and Tardos proved this estimate on the way to improved bounds for the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane. Their explicit five-entry and nine-entry estimates give, by the same proof, the thresholds 132169\frac{132}{169} and 368471\frac{368}{471} in place of q∗q_{*}, and

Q5​(t)=32​t+100211−42​t,Q9​(t)=88​t+280589−118​tQ_{5}(t)=\frac{32t+100}{211-42t},\qquad Q_{9}(t)=\frac{88t+280}{589-118t}

in place of Q⁡(t)Q(t) for 1≤t≤321\leq t\leq\frac{3}{2}. The proof keeps the threshold q∗q_{*} independent of the source dimension, while the scale at which its estimates apply may depend on the source and pin measures. The source dimension enters through the estimate in Section 6 and its iteration in Section 8.5. The proof outline below describes which information about the two points these estimates retain.

Allowing either endpoint to serve as the pin yields a larger gain in the exponent.

Theorem 1.2 (Unpinned distance sets).

There is an absolute constant 0<η0<3400<\eta_{0}<\frac{3}{40} such that every analytic E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with t=dimHE>1t=\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1 satisfies

dimHΔ​E≥max⁡{45+η0,Y⁡(t),R⁡(t)},\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E\geq\max\left\{\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0},Y(t),R(t)\right\}, (1.1)

where S0=11−414=1.149218​…S_{0}=\frac{11-\sqrt{41}}{4}=1.149218\ldots and

Y⁡(t)={t2−2​t+52​t2−7​t+10,1≤t≤S0,78,t≥S0,R⁡(t)=min⁡{1,t⁡(4−t)5−t}.Y(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{t^{2}-2t+5}{2t^{2}-7t+10},&1\leq t\leq S_{0},\\[5.0pt] \displaystyle\frac{7}{8},&t\geq S_{0},\end{cases}\qquad R(t)=\min\left\{1,\frac{t(4-t)}{5-t}\right\}.

In particular, dimHΔ​E≥78\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E\geq\frac{7}{8} for t≥S0t\geq S_{0}.

The function YY is increasing on [1,S0][1,S_{0}], with Y⁡(1)=45Y(1)=\frac{4}{5} and Y⁡(S0)=78Y(S_{0})=\frac{7}{8}. For every fixed 1<t≤S01<t\leq S_{0}, its gain over 45\frac{4}{5} is explicit:

Y⁡(t)−45=3​(t−1)​(5−t)5​(2​t2−7​t+10)>0.Y(t)-\frac{4}{5}=\frac{3(t-1)(5-t)}{5(2t^{2}-7t+10)}>0.

This gain tends to zero as t↘1t\searrow 1. The constant η0\eta_{0} provides a uniform positive gain throughout t>1t>1. The bound R⁡(t)R(t) follows from Fiedler–Stull [7, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2]; it is also recovered by letting pp increase to tt in Theorem 1.5 below. It exceeds Y⁡(t)Y(t) when t>39−40116=1.1859​…t>\frac{39-\sqrt{401}}{16}=1.1859\ldots. Table 1 records the comparison with earlier unpinned estimates.

Two arguments enter Theorem 1.2. The reciprocal partition estimate in Section 10, combined with the source-dimension iteration, proves Y⁡(t)Y(t). The fixed gain η0\eta_{0} requires more. At the scalar endpoint, both profiles have a common interval of excess information. Section 13 proves this rigidity statement, and Section 29 uses the common source measure to rule out the resulting geometric configuration. The compactness argument does not assign a numerical value to η0\eta_{0}. This constant is chosen independently of the set and its measures. The starting precision in the finite argument may depend on the measures, as explained in Remark 21.2. The elementary arguments in Appendices B and C illustrate the first interaction between the two endpoint estimates.

There is a stronger pinned conclusion if Hausdorff dimension of the image is replaced by lower box dimension. For a bounded set FF, let Nr​(F)N_{r}(F) be the least number of open balls of radius rr covering FF, and define

dim¯B​F=lim infn→∞log2⁡N2−n​(F)n.\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}F=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}N_{2^{-n}}(F)}{n}.

Put

L⁡(s)=min⁡{3​s+15,78},L∗​(s)=max⁡{45+η0,L⁡(s)}.L(s)=\min\left\{\frac{3s+1}{5},\frac{7}{8}\right\},\qquad L_{*}(s)=\max\left\{\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0},L(s)\right\}. (1.2)
Theorem 1.3 (Pinned lower box dimension).

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be compact, and let μ\mu be any nonzero finite ss-Frostman measure supported on EE, with s>1s>1. Then

dim¯B​Δx​E≥L∗​(s)for μ-almost every ​x.\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}\Delta_{x}E\geq L_{*}(s)\quad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x. (1.3)

After normalizing μ\mu to have mass one, for every q<L∗​(s)q<L_{*}(s) and M>0M>0 one has

μ⁡{x∈E:N2−n​(Δx​E)<2q​n}≤n−M\mu\{x\in E:N_{2^{-n}}(\Delta_{x}E)<2^{qn}\}\leq n^{-M} (1.4)

for all sufficiently large nn. The starting precision may depend on E,μ,s,q,ME,\mu,s,q,M.

The exponent ss belongs to the specified measure. No lower mass bound or equality of Hausdorff and packing dimensions is assumed. The explicit bound L⁡(s)L(s) reaches 78\frac{7}{8} at s=98s=\frac{9}{8}. The proof chooses two bad pins whose complexity profiles nearly agree at the precision under consideration. The pair may change with the precision; Section 26 establishes the uniform estimates needed for this selection.

Corollary 1.4 (Internal lower-box exceptional sets).

For every bounded E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2},

dimH{x∈E:dim¯B​Δx​E<45+η0}≤1.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{x\in E:\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}\Delta_{x}E<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}\}\leq 1. (1.5)

For 45≤q<78\frac{4}{5}\leq q<\frac{7}{8}, one also has

dimH{x∈E:dim¯B​Δx​E≤q}≤5​q−13,dimH{x∈E:dim¯B​Δx​E<78}≤98.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{x\in E:\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}\Delta_{x}E\leq q\}\leq\frac{5q-1}{3},\qquad\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{x\in E:\underline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}\Delta_{x}E<\frac{7}{8}\}\leq\frac{9}{8}.

No measurability assumption on EE is required.

These are internal lower-box statements. Theorem 1.1 concerns Hausdorff dimension and pins anywhere in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Under the common dyadic mass law of Theorem D.2, matching profiles persist along all sequences of precisions, and the bound L∗​(s)L_{*}(s) also holds for pinned Hausdorff dimension. Appendix D treats that case.

Fiedler and Stull combine the dimension parameters of the two endpoints into a common minimum in part of their argument, and observe in footnote 7 that keeping them separate could improve the bound at the cost of more calculations [7, §4.3, footnote 7]. The next theorem carries out this refinement, keeping the source dimension dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E and the exceptional-set parameter pp separate.

Theorem 1.5 (Pinned exceptional sets).

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be analytic with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1, and let 1≤p<dimHE1\leq p<\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E. Put

B⁡(p,t)=min⁡{1,p+t⁡(3−p)5−p}.B(p,t)=\min\left\{1,\frac{p+t(3-p)}{5-p}\right\}.

Then

dimH{x∈ℝ2:dimHΔx​E<B⁡(p,dimHE)}≤p.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E<B(p,\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E)\}\leq p.

In particular, dimHΔx​E≥min⁡{1,14+dimHE2}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq\min\{1,\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E}{2}\} outside an exceptional set of dimension at most one.

The proof of Theorem 1.1 controls the directions of the source points as seen from each pin. Controlling also the directions of the pins as seen from each source point leads to a second estimate, which is better when Srel<dimHE<SfS_{\mathrm{rel}}<\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E<S_{f}. Let

Srel\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{rel}} =1+5−8​α∗−3​α∗26​α∗2−48​α∗+30=1.124334​…,\displaystyle=1+\frac{5-8\alpha_{*}-3\alpha_{*}^{2}}{6\alpha_{*}^{2}-48\alpha_{*}+30}=1.124334\ldots,
Sswitch\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{switch}} =1+5​α∗2−α∗−110​α∗2+2​α∗−6=1.175876​…,\displaystyle=1+\frac{5\alpha_{*}^{2}-\alpha_{*}-1}{10\alpha_{*}^{2}+2\alpha_{*}-6}=1.175876\ldots,
Sf\displaystyle S_{f} =1+6+10​α∗−(6+10​α∗)2−48​α∗​(1+2​α∗)24​α∗=1.197246​….\displaystyle=1+\frac{6+10\alpha_{*}-\sqrt{(6+10\alpha_{*})^{2}-48\alpha_{*}(1+2\alpha_{*})}}{24\alpha_{*}}=1.197246\ldots.

For Srel≤t≤SfS_{\mathrm{rel}}\leq t\leq S_{f}, define

Qrel(t)=min{1−5​(1−α∗)​(3−2​t)6​{1+2​α∗+2​(1−2​α∗)​t},1−3−2​t4+6​α∗−4​α∗​t}.Q_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)=\min\Biggl\{1-\frac{5(1-\alpha_{*})(3-2t)}{6\{1+2\alpha_{*}+2(1-2\alpha_{*})t\}},\quad 1-\frac{3-2t}{4+6\alpha_{*}-4\alpha_{*}t}\Biggr\}. (1.6)

The first expression is the smaller one up to SswitchS_{\mathrm{switch}}. The second is the smaller one after that point.

Theorem 1.6 (A second pinned bound).

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be analytic with dimHE∈[Srel,Sf]\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E\in[S_{\mathrm{rel}},S_{f}]. Then

dimH{x∈ℝ2:dimHΔx​E<Qrel​(dimHE)}≤1.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E<Q_{\mathrm{rel}}(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E)\}\leq 1.

1.1 Earlier results and the inputs to this paper

Falconer proved positive Lebesgue measure of the planar distance set above dimension 32\frac{3}{2} [6]. Wolff lowered this threshold to 43\frac{4}{3} [36]. Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang proved the positive-measure conclusion above 54\frac{5}{4}, including a pinned conclusion with a pin in EE [11]. The present paper concerns dimensions close to one, where the dimension problem remains open without additional assumptions.

Bourgain’s work, following Katz–Tao, gave a uniform improvement over the elementary exponent 12\frac{1}{2} at source dimension one [2, 15]. For sources of dimension greater than one, Keleti–Shmerkin obtained the universal unpinned bound 3754\frac{37}{54} and the pinned bound 23​dimHE\frac{2}{3}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E outside a set of pins of dimension at most one when 1<dimHE≤321<\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E\leq\frac{3}{2} [17, Theorems 1.4 and 1.1]. Shmerkin improved the universal unpinned exponent to 4057\frac{40}{57} and obtained the pinned exponent 2942\frac{29}{42} outside a set of pins of dimension at most one [30, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2]. Their treatment of information across scales provides a measure-theoretic precursor to our use of information at intermediate scales.

The point-to-set principle of J. H. Lutz and N. Lutz expresses Hausdorff dimension through the description lengths of individual points [21]. Lutz–Stull developed estimates for these description lengths under orthogonal projection, the map z↦z⋅vz\mapsto z\cdot v for a unit vector vv [22]. Stull used this approach to obtain the pinned bound quoted above [33]. With the covering number Nr​(F)N_{r}(F) defined above, the upper box dimension of FF is dim¯B​F=lim supr↘0log⁡Nr​(F)log⁡(1r)\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}F=\limsup_{r\searrow 0}\frac{\log N_{r}(F)}{\log(\frac{1}{r})}. The packing dimension is

dimPE=infE⊆⋃iEisupidim¯B​Ei,\dim_{\mathrm{P}}E=\inf_{E\subseteq\bigcup_{i}E_{i}}\sup_{i}\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}E_{i},

where the infimum is over countable covers by bounded sets [23, Chapter 5]. Fiedler–Stull refined the scale partitions and retained both Hausdorff and packing dimension parameters [7, Theorems 1 and 5]. At planar packing dimension two, their expression becomes min⁡{1,d⁡(4−d)5−d}\min\{1,\frac{d(4-d)}{5-d}\} for 1<d<dimHE1<d<\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E, with an exceptional-pin dimension bound dd. Sections 3 and 4 specify the information estimates retained from these proofs. References to their equation and lemma numbers use the listed arXiv versions: [33], v2, and [7], v1. Appendix A contains the retained prefix calculation and its endpoint case.

Liu’s L2L^{2} method provides additional dimension-dependent estimates [19]. At exceptional-pin dimension one, it yields the threshold min⁡{1,dimHE−13}\min\{1,\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E-\frac{1}{3}\}. It also implies

supx∈EdimHΔx​E≥min⁡{4​dimHE−23,1}.\sup_{x\in E}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq\min\left\{\frac{4\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E-2}{3},1\right\}.

The supremum is needed because of the correction to the pinned endpoint in [19]. The pin achieving an exponent close to the right side may depend on that exponent. Liu states these results for compact EE. They extend to analytic EE by inner approximation with compact subsets.

Regularity can lead to stronger conclusions. A compact set EE of positive diameter is ss-Ahlfors–David regular if it supports a finite Borel measure μ\mu with support equal to the set and c​rs≤μ⁡(B⁡(z,r))≤C​rscr^{s}\leq\mu(B(z,r))\leq Cr^{s} for all points zz of the set and 0<r≤diam⁡E0<r\leq\operatorname{diam}E. The constants are positive and independent of z,rz,r. Orponen proved that the distance sets of such planar sets have packing dimension one when s≥1s\geq 1 [26]. Shmerkin obtained full pinned Hausdorff dimension when dimHE=dimPE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E=\dim_{\mathrm{P}}E>1 [29]. Fiedler–Stull cover further ranges of these two dimensions [7, 8]. Shmerkin–Wang proved that for every d≥2d\geq 2 and every Borel E⊆ℝdE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with dimHE=dimPE=d2\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E=\dim_{\mathrm{P}}E=\frac{d}{2}, supx∈EdimHΔx​E=1\sup_{x\in E}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E=1 [31, Theorem 1.4]. Liu recently proved that if E,F⊂ℝ2E,F\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} are Borel, dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1, dimHF=dimPF\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F=\dim_{\mathrm{P}}F and dimHE+dimHF>2\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E+\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F>2, then Δx​E\Delta_{x}E has positive Lebesgue measure for some x∈Fx\in F [20, Theorem 1.1]. At source dimension at most one, Cholak, Csörnyei, N. Lutz, P. Lutz, Mayordomo and Stull proved the pinned supremum bound 34​dimHE\frac{3}{4}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E for analytic EE [3, Theorem 6].

A closely related combination of algorithmic information and incidence geometry appears in recent work of Csörnyei and Stull [5]. They extend the Ren–Wang incidence estimate to hyperplanes in higher dimensions and prove that, for every Borel set E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with dimHE>d2\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>\frac{d}{2}, where d=3d=3 or 44,

supx∈EdimHΔx​E≥23.\sup_{x\in E}\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq\frac{2}{3}.

Their proof converts incidence estimates into conditional Kolmogorov complexity bounds and combines them over intervals of scales. These intervals are selected by a decomposition of complexity functions based on Jones’s traveling salesman theorem [5, Section 5]. In dimension two, their incidence theorem specializes to the Ren–Wang estimate used here. Our planar improvement combines information retained at both endpoints with a common source measure to obtain incompatible lower and upper counts for rich perpendicular bisectors.

Our geometric argument uses further inputs. The radial projection about xx sends y≠xy\neq x to its direction πx​(y)=y−x|y−x|\pi_{x}(y)=\frac{y-x}{|y-x|} on the unit circle S1={z∈ℝ2:|z|=1}S^{1}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:|z|=1\}. Orponen’s theorem controls the distribution of these directions [25]. The crossing lemma, in the circle-drawing tradition of Székely, turns many circle incidences into repeated pairs [34]. The restricted-sum estimate of Katz–Tardos bounds from below the number of bisector directions produced by rows, meaning ordered lists of source points assigned to a common circle [16], and the max-flow min-cut theorem of Ford–Fulkerson turns this into a simultaneous choice of one direction per row [9]. The Furstenberg estimate of Ren–Wang bounds the number of rich bisector tubes from below [28], and the incidence estimate of Fu–Gan–Ren for rectangularly spaced balls bounds it from above [10]. We state the precise forms needed when they enter the proof.

A related use of rigidity occurs in the work of Héra, Shmerkin and Yavicoli on Furstenberg sets [12, Section 4.1]. There, a configuration close to the elementary bound has a restricted incidence structure, which is incompatible with Bourgain’s projection theorem. Here the starting constraint is equality in the reciprocal information estimates. It forces a common interval of excess information, from which we obtain rich bisectors. The final contradiction uses the geometric estimates specified above.

Several features of the proof also have counterparts in work on the Erdős similarity conjecture. This conjecture asks whether, for every infinite A⊂ℝA\subset\mathbb{R}, there is a measurable set of positive Lebesgue measure containing no set x+λ​Ax+\lambda A with x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and λ≠0\lambda\neq 0. Shmerkin and Yavicoli [32, Section 3.2] use probabilistic selection to construct one small set whose sums with every member of a prescribed family cover a fixed region. The cost of treating the family simultaneously is logarithmic in the number of discrete tests. The same requirement of a common choice enters Lemmas 17.1 and 17.7 below. The source sample must serve every retained pin, and the pin sample must preserve the witnesses for every retained source pair. Separate choices would lose the shared incidence structure.

A second connection concerns approximate coincidences of sums. Mora Cuellar, Iosevich, Kulkarni, Rojas Aravena and Yavicoli [24, Section 3.2] bound their number for two lacunary sequences, meaning positive sequences (aj)(a_{j}) satisfying aj+1≤q​aja_{j+1}\leq qa_{j} for some fixed 0<q<10<q<1. Their estimate allows many separated sums to be extracted without requiring the two sequences to occupy different ranges of scales. Here sums of angular coordinates determine bisector directions, so a related counting question enters Section 18. Our angular rows need not be lacunary, and we use the restricted-sum estimate of Katz–Tardos under the hypotheses available to us.

The lattice construction of Iosevich and Yavicoli [14, Section 2] illustrates a further role for information across scales. Sufficient branching between successive lattice scales allows the construction of an infinite set AA whose triple sumset A+A+A={a1+a2+a3:a1,a2,a3∈A}A+A+A=\{a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}:a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in A\} lies in the limiting set. In the present argument, excess information over a common interval of scales produces the mass bounds from which the rich bisectors are extracted. Both arguments use how branching is distributed across scales. The arithmetic alignment of the lattice construction, however, is additional structure that a general Frostman measure need not possess.

There is also a comparison with the work of Iosevich, Kulkarni, Mora Cuéllar, Rojas Aravena and Yavicoli on Rajchman measures [13, Lemma 2.3 and Proposition 3.2]. A Rajchman probability measure is a Borel probability measure whose Fourier–Stieltjes transform tends to zero at infinity. For such a measure with compact support, that qualitative decay yields a density statement modulo one for all sufficiently large dilates of the support. This leads to a single set excluding all nontrivial affine copies of that support. Our endpoint stability argument likewise separates a qualitative limiting statement from the finite-scale geometry, with the measure affecting the starting precision. Here the required input is supplied by information profiles and incidence estimates. No Rajchman hypothesis is imposed. These comparisons describe related uses of selection, additive structure and scale information. The estimates needed for the distance problem are proved below.

1.2 The bisector results as separate statements

For distinct y,z∈ℝ2y,z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, their perpendicular bisector is

ℬ⁡(y,z)={x∈ℝ2:|x−y|=|x−z|}.\mathcal{B}(y,z)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:|x-y|=|x-z|\}.

The perpendicular bisectors ℬ⁡(y,z)\mathcal{B}(y,z) defined above will be treated as a family of lines. Write a line as Ln,c={z∈ℝ2:n⋅z=c}L_{n,c}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:n\cdot z=c\}, where n∈S1n\in S^{1} is a unit normal and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} is its offset. The parameters (n,c)(n,c) and (−n,−c)(-n,-c) represent the same unoriented line. We give this space the metric

dist⁡(Ln,c,Ln′,c′)=min⁡{|n−n′|+|c−c′|,|n+n′|+|c+c′|}.\operatorname{dist}(L_{n,c},L_{n^{\prime},c^{\prime}})=\min\{|n-n^{\prime}|+|c-c^{\prime}|,|n+n^{\prime}|+|c+c^{\prime}|\}.

The dimension of a family of lines is taken in this metric. A tube is a neighborhood of a line of specified width. Relative to a finite pin set, a tube is called kk-rich if it contains at least kk pins.

Several geometric statements below are independent of the information theory. Here the Hausdorff dimension of a family of lines is computed in the space of affine lines equipped with the metric above, not as the dimension of their union in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Proposition 15.1 establishes the elementary identity

dimH{ℬ⁡(y,z):z∈F}=dimHFfor ​y∉F.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{\mathcal{B}(y,z):z\in F\}=\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F\qquad\text{for }y\notin F.

It follows that the set of all bisectors determined by EE has Hausdorff dimension at least dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E when this dimension is positive. The reflection map proves this identity directly. It supplies a Hausdorff-dimension statement to accompany the finite results.

The finite geometric estimates used below have their own hypotheses. They concern approximate circle drawings, rows of points with rich bisectors, the distribution of their directions, and rich tubes for point sets with controlled spacing. These statements can also be used independently of the description-length estimates below.

1.3 How the proofs work

A short description of a distance places constraints on both endpoints. The estimates of Stull and Fiedler–Stull express these constraints at each scale. We retain their dependence on the information at both endpoints. In the unpinned problem, the resulting inequalities can be applied in both directions. They force the scalar bound 45\frac{4}{5} and identify the profiles near equality. For a prescribed pin they need not do so. They instead force a particular distribution of pin and source mass, which we use to construct a finite configuration of circles and points.

The geometric contradiction concerns one family of perpendicular bisectors. Each bisector has many pins near it. The source points on the circles provide many possible bisector directions, and Katz–Tardos and Ren–Wang turn those choices into a lower bound for the number of distinct bisectors. The distribution of the pins provides an upper bound for the same number. The improvement occurs when these bounds are incompatible. Thus information theory determines the configuration that a small distance set would require, and incidence geometry rules out that configuration.

There are two reasons for keeping more information than a single dimension exponent. The first is that information may accumulate unevenly across scales. Information missing on one interval has to appear on another, and the projection estimates can use its location. The second is that all pins see the same source set. A mass bound for one source measure can be used simultaneously in the circle drawings at different pins. Choosing a separate source measure for each pin would lose the shared vertices needed for the counting argument. We now explain both points and how the estimates fit together.

Let x,y∈ℝ2x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be distinct. The line segment joining them is

[x,y]={(1−t′)​x+t′​y:t′∈[0,1]},[x,y]=\{(1-t^{\prime})x+t^{\prime}y:t^{\prime}\in[0,1]\},

and its length is |x−y||x-y|. We measure information by program length. Fix a universal binary machine with prefix-free programs, meaning that no admissible program is a proper initial segment of another. An oracle A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N} supplies background information. The machine may ask whether an integer belongs to AA without including the answer in its program. The oracle is fixed before the points and the sequence of precisions are chosen.

For z∈ℝmz\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, let KrA​(z)K_{r}^{A}(z) be the length of a shortest program, using AA, that locates zz within distance 2−r2^{-r}. The notation KrA,x​(|x−y|)K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|) also supplies the complete pin xx, so the program describes only the distance. Section 2.2 specifies the encodings and the distinction between supplying a whole point and supplying only a coarse approximation. These are the conventions of [18, 33, 7].

To record where the information lies, choose terminal precisions rj→∞r_{j}\to\infty and write u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] for a fraction of terminal precision. Along a common subsequence we have

f⁡(u)\displaystyle f(u) =limj→∞K⌊u​rj⌋A​(y)rj,\displaystyle=\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{K_{\lfloor ur_{j}\rfloor}^{A}(y)}{r_{j}}, g⁡(u)\displaystyle g(u) =limj→∞K⌊u​rj⌋A​(x)rj,\displaystyle=\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{K_{\lfloor ur_{j}\rfloor}^{A}(x)}{r_{j}},
dx​(u)\displaystyle d_{x}(u) =limj→∞K⌊u​rj⌋A,x​(|x−y|)rj,\displaystyle=\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{K_{\lfloor ur_{j}\rfloor}^{A,x}(|x-y|)}{r_{j}}, dy​(u)\displaystyle d_{y}(u) =limj→∞K⌊u​rj⌋A,y​(|x−y|)rj.\displaystyle=\lim_{j\to\infty}\frac{K_{\lfloor ur_{j}\rfloor}^{A,y}(|x-y|)}{r_{j}}.

Here ⌊v⌋\lfloor v\rfloor and ⌈v⌉\lceil v\rceil denote integer rounding down and up, respectively, and the complexities at precision zero are set equal to zero. These functions are the information profiles. The source profile is ff, the pin profile is gg, and the distance has one profile for each choice of pin. The points remain fixed. Section 2.4 proves uniform convergence of all four profiles along one subsequence.

The pairs used in the proof have directions requiring nearly one bit per unit of precision, even after either endpoint is supplied. Also, supplying one endpoint does not substantially shorten a description of the other. Orponen’s radial projection theorem and the measure-coding argument allow us to select such pairs. Under these hypotheses, the prefix estimate reads

dx​(u)≥u2+f⁡(u)4.d_{x}(u)\geq\frac{u}{2}+\frac{f(u)}{4}.

It says how much information already accumulated at the source must have reached the distance by scale uu. At the lowest profile f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u, this is dx​(u)≥3​u4d_{x}(u)\geq\frac{3u}{4}. At the largest planar profile f⁡(u)=2​uf(u)=2u, it is dx​(u)≥ud_{x}(u)\geq u. To improve the first bound, we must use how the profiles change between scales.

This is the purpose of the interval transfer estimate. Suppose a coarse location of yy and its distance from xx are known. Another possible source point zz must be near that location and satisfy |x−z|=|x−y||x-z|=|x-y|. Thus xx lies on the perpendicular bisector of [y,z][y,z]. The points y,zy,z determine a projection of xx, at a precision governed by their separation. The projection estimates of Stull and Fiedler–Stull therefore put a lower bound on the description length of every competitor zz. If all competitors require many bits, the distance and the coarse location must together contain many bits as well.

The transfer threshold Hf,g​(a,b)H_{f,g}(a,b) in (4.4) is the least of these competitor costs, capped by the source information at the terminal scale. Lemma 4.1 states the resulting bound

dx​(b)−dx​(a)≥[Hf,g​(a,b)−f⁡(a)]+.d_{x}(b)-d_{x}(a)\geq[H_{f,g}(a,b)-f(a)]_{+}.

The subtraction of f⁡(a)f(a) accounts for the coarse source information already supplied. Partitioning the projection calculation into intervals with different patterns of information growth strengthens HH to H^\widehat{H} in Lemma 7.2. Both estimates retain the two endpoint profiles.

For the unpinned problem, a short description of |x−y||x-y| remains short after either endpoint is supplied. We may therefore assume that both dx​(1)d_{x}(1) and dy​(1)d_{y}(1) are small and use the transfer inequalities in both orientations. A common cutoff is a scale after which all competitors in either orientation cost at least a specified amount of information, called the transfer level. Prefix and transfer then bound both endpoint profiles from below at the cutoff. Their Lipschitz bounds carry some of this information to earlier scales, where it strengthens the next transfer estimate.

The final contradiction uses the least possible common cutoff. At this scale one orientation must have a competitor whose cost equals the transfer level. Otherwise the cutoff could be moved slightly earlier. We retain the two separate endpoint excesses, apply the partition estimates in both directions, and return to this equality. The resulting lower bound exceeds the value allowed by the equality. Section 10 proves in this way that dx​(1),dy​(1)d_{x}(1),d_{y}(1) cannot both be smaller than 45\frac{4}{5}. Keeping the source dimension in the transfer level also yields Y⁡(dimHE)Y(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E) in Section 11. The fixed-pair construction and the point-to-set principle in Section 5 convert these conclusions into bounds for dimHΔ​E\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E. Proposition 31.1 shows why the stated scalar system stops at 45\frac{4}{5}. At equality, however, the profiles have much more structure. They grow at the maximal rate before 15\frac{1}{5} and remain above u+15u+\frac{1}{5} until 35\frac{3}{5}. This interval of excess information allows the geometric count to pass the scalar endpoint. Compactness makes the same contradiction valid in a fixed neighborhood of 45\frac{4}{5}.

For a prescribed pin, this argument has a specific failure. A description that is short when xx is supplied may be long when only yy is supplied. Thus dx​(1)d_{x}(1) may be small while dy​(1)d_{y}(1) is large. Proposition 7.3 exhibits abstract profiles satisfying all the scalar inequalities with dx​(1)d_{x}(1) arbitrarily close to 34\frac{3}{4} and dy​(1)=1d_{y}(1)=1. The pinned improvement must therefore use a relation among many pairs.

Suppose that the set of pins where the proposed bound fails has Hausdorff dimension greater than one. We choose a source probability measure μ\mu and a pin probability measure ν\nu, supported on separated compact sets, both with Frostman exponent greater than one. A relation of pairs is a Borel set GG in the product of these supports. Its fiber at a pin is Gx={y:(x,y)∈G}G_{x}=\{y:(x,y)\in G\}. We retain one such relation with

(ν×μ)​(G)=∫μ⁡(Gx)​𝑑ν​(x)>0.(\nu\times\mu)(G)=\int\mu(G_{x})d\nu(x)>0.

The radial projection theorem supplies bounded angular densities on this relation after restriction. It is these restrictions of the same original measures that are used throughout the geometry.

Fix a proposed distance bound qq. For every pair in the retained relation, the inequality KnA,x​(|x−y|)≤q​nK_{n}^{A,x}(|x-y|)\leq qn holds at infinitely many precisions. These precisions may differ from pair to pair. Lemma 20.4 finds infinitely many common precisions at which the pairs satisfying this inequality have total mass at least n−2n^{-2}. At one such precision there are at most 2q​n+O⁡(log⁡n)2^{qn+O(\log n)} occupied radius bins per pin. Indeed, there are only that many short programs, and an approximation to a radius identifies its bin up to a bounded choice. Thus the small distance set produces many source incidences on relatively few circles at each pin.

The profile argument supplies two further facts at these precisions. First, g⁡(u)−u≥Wg(u)-u\geq W throughout an interval [u−,u+][u_{-},u_{+}] of controlled length, with W>0W>0. This is the pin plateau. The profile need not be constant on that interval. Coding the pin measure turns the plateau into upper bounds for pin mass over a range of scales. Second, the source reaches a prescribed amount of information early enough that a lower bound for the radius complexity remains after a coarse source location has been supplied. This is the source-parent estimate in Section 14.

The cancellation in that second fact is worth displaying. Set δ=2−n\delta=2^{-n}, and let CC be a dyadic parent square containing yy. A dyadic square has the form 2−k([i,i+1)×[j,j+1))2^{-k}([i,i+1)\times[j,j+1)), and a parent is a containing square at a coarser level. If JJ is the radius interval of length δ\delta containing |x−y||x-y|, put

pC,J=μ⁡{z∈C:|x−z|∈J}.p_{C,J}=\mu\{z\in C:|x-z|\in J\}.

The transfer estimate, the source coding identity, and the code for the radial distribution of μ|Cμ⁡(C)\frac{\mu|_{C}}{\mu(C)} imply, up to the selectable small errors,

λ​n+log2⁡μ⁡(C)≤KnA,x​(|x−y|∣C)≤−log2⁡pC,J+log2⁡μ⁡(C).\lambda n+\log_{2}\mu(C)\leq K_{n}^{A,x}(|x-y|\mid C)\leq-\log_{2}p_{C,J}+\log_{2}\mu(C).

The parent mass cancels, leaving pC,J≤δλp_{C,J}\leq\delta^{\lambda} at leading exponent order. Proposition 14.2 states the precise bound with its error tolerance. It holds for the original source measure in every occupied parent and annulus. Thus many incidences cannot all be hidden in one small part of a circle. If the source dimension is larger, its stronger profile lower bound permits a larger transfer level λ\lambda, as proved in Section 8.5.

We now select source squares once for all pins and use their centers as vertices. An assigned incidence records a retained pair, its source square, and its radius bin. The vertex lies within O⁡(δ)O(\delta) of the associated circle. The source-parent mass bound controls how many assigned vertices can occur in one parent on that circle. The common-scale mass lower bound allows the selections to lose fixed powers of nn. Their logarithms are o⁡(n)o(n), so they do not change the limiting exponents.

Join consecutive assigned vertices along the circles. A drawing with many edges but controlled crossings must repeat many source pairs. A repeated pair y,zy,z is seen from many circle centers. Those centers lie within distance O⁡(δ|y−z|)O(\frac{\delta}{|y-z|}) of the perpendicular bisector of [y,z][y,z]. A witnessing pin is a pin to which both source vertices were assigned on the same circle. We have therefore constructed bisector tubes with many witnesses, as illustrated in Figure 1. The drawing and pruning arguments also provide short lists of vertices on a circle, called rows, from which pairs can be chosen.

The lower count uses the freedom in this choice. On an exact circle, if two source points have angles θi,θj\theta_{i},\theta_{j} about the pin, their bisector direction is θi+θj2\frac{\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}}{2} modulo π\pi. Our approximate circles obey the corresponding relation with controlled errors. After removing repeated angular entries, the Katz–Tardos restricted-sum estimate bounds the number of available directions for collections of rows. A large total number of directions would not by itself suffice, since they might cluster in a short angular interval. The matching argument in Section 18 chooses one pair per row while controlling the directions at every intermediate scale. Ren–Wang’s Furstenberg theorem can then be applied to the pins and their selected tube directions. It forces many distinct bisector tubes.

The first upper count uses the same tubes and their witnessing pins. The pin plateau controls concentration in rectangles. The sampling argument of Section 19 converts that control into the rectangular occupancy required by Fu–Gan–Ren. Their incidence theorem limits how many distinct tubes can each contain the required number of pins. Comparing this upper count with the Furstenberg lower count proves Q⁡(dimHE)Q(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E), including the universal bound q∗q_{*}.

For the second upper count, keep the angular bound as seen from the source endpoint as well as from the generating pin. For a source pair separated by ℓ\ell, a length-DD portion of its bisector subtends an angle of order ℓ​D\ell D from that endpoint, in our separated regions. The reverse angular bound therefore limits how many witnesses of this pair can lie in one small square. A rich pair must have witnesses in many such squares. Lemma 23.2 retains the dependence on their coarse tube occupancy and turns this additional distribution information into a second upper count. It improves the pinned bound to Qrel​(dimHE)Q_{\mathrm{rel}}(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E) on the interval specified in Theorem 1.6.

The distinction between these counts is useful. Katz–Tardos controls the choices of directions, Ren–Wang turns distributed directions into a lower count, and the upper incidence estimates use the distribution of witnesses. All three refer to the same finite configuration. Figure 2 records these dependencies.

Keeping the pin Frostman exponent in the same lower count yields the quantitative exceptional-set estimates of Section 25. Appendix D combines the matching scalar estimate with the geometric argument when almost every pair has matching information profiles. The elementary scalar proofs are retained in Appendices B and C. Section 31 identifies the limitations of the scalar inequalities and the separate geometric comparisons. Appendix E treats their joint optimization.

2   Preliminaries

We collect the geometric conventions and the definitions of information used in the proofs. The basic object is a shortest program producing a rational point within a prescribed error. All programs below use the same optimal machine. The pair (x,y)(x,y) and the background oracle AA remain fixed as the error tends to zero. This is what will allow a statement about individual points to imply a Hausdorff-dimension bound.

2.1 Sets, measures, and geometric scales

The Hausdorff measure ℋs\mathcal{H}^{s}, Hausdorff and packing dimensions, and Frostman and Ahlfors–David bounds were defined in the introduction. See also [23, Chapters 4, 5, 8]. We will use countable stability of Hausdorff dimension. The dimension of a countable union is the supremum of the dimensions of its members [23, Chapter 4].

The restriction μ|F\mu|_{F} is the measure B↦μ⁡(B∩F)B\mapsto\mu(B\cap F), and its normalization is μ|Fμ⁡(F)\frac{\mu|_{F}}{\mu(F)} when 0<μ⁡(F)<∞0<\mu(F)<\infty.

Frostman’s lemma says that every analytic set of dimension greater than ss contains a compact subset carrying an ss-Frostman probability measure [23, Chapter 8]. Its energy

It​(μ)=∬|x−y|−t​𝑑μ​(x)​𝑑μ​(y)I_{t}(\mu)=\iint|x-y|^{-t}d\mu(x)d\mu(y)

is finite for 0<t<s0<t<s. We apply the radial projection πx\pi_{x} only on source regions separated from xx. For a measurable map TT, its pushforward T∗​μT_{*}\mu is defined by (T∗​μ)​(B)=μ⁡(T−1​(B))(T_{*}\mu)(B)=\mu(T^{-1}(B)). A measure is absolutely continuous with respect to another if it assigns zero mass to every set of zero mass for the other. A density of ν\nu with respect to μ\mu is a nonnegative measurable function hh such that ν⁡(B)=∫Bh​𝑑μ\nu(B)=\int_{B}hd\mu for every measurable BB. This is also called the Radon–Nikodym derivative. Angular Lebesgue measure means arclength on S1S^{1}. A bound (πx)∗​μ≤L​ℋ1(\pi_{x})_{*}\mu\leq L\mathcal{H}^{1} means that every arc JJ has preimage mass at most L​|J|L|J|, where |J||J| is its length. For a Borel relation GG we use the fibers Gx={y∈ℝ2:(x,y)∈G}G_{x}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:(x,y)\in G\} and Gy={x∈ℝ2:(x,y)∈G}G^{y}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:(x,y)\in G\} and the pair mass (ν×μ)​(G)(\nu\times\mu)(G).

For a set F⊆ℝmF\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, dist⁡(z,F)=infw∈F|z−w|\operatorname{dist}(z,F)=\inf_{w\in F}|z-w| and F(r)={z∈ℝm:dist⁡(z,F)<r}F^{(r)}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:\operatorname{dist}(z,F)<r\}. A set is rr-separated if distinct points have distance at least rr. A fixed enlargement of a square is its concentric dilation by a fixed factor. We use the Hausdorff metric on nonempty compact sets,

dH(K,K′)=max{supz∈Kdist(z,K′),supw∈K′dist(w,K)}.d_{\mathrm{H}}(K,K^{\prime})=\max\left\{\sup_{z\in K}\operatorname{dist}(z,K^{\prime}),\quad\sup_{w\in K^{\prime}}\operatorname{dist}(w,K)\right\}.

A map is LL-Lipschitz if it increases distances by at most a factor LL. It is bi-Lipschitz if it is one-to-one and it and its inverse are Lipschitz. Such maps preserve Hausdorff dimension [23, Chapter 7]. A lower envelope for a function is another function lying below it at every argument. We also call a lower bound a barrier, and a constant lower bound a floor. For functions on a fixed compact interval, ‖f−g‖∞=supu|f⁡(u)−g⁡(u)|\|f-g\|_{\infty}=\sup_{u}|f(u)-g(u)| is their uniform distance. A functional is lower semicontinuous if its value at a limit is at most the lower limit of its values along every convergent sequence. Upper semicontinuity reverses this inequality and uses the upper limit. For sets RnR_{n}, the set lim supnRn=⋂N⋃n≥NRn\limsup_{n}R_{n}=\bigcap_{N}\bigcup_{n\geq N}R_{n} consists of points belonging to infinitely many RnR_{n}.

We write [t]+=max⁡{t,0}[t]_{+}=\max\{t,0\}, #​F\#F for cardinality, and 1G1_{G} for the indicator of GG, equal to one on GG and zero outside it. Logarithms are to base two. Dyadic cubes in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} are the half-open products ∏j=1m[2−n​kj,2−n​(kj+1))\prod_{j=1}^{m}[2^{-n}k_{j},2^{-n}(k_{j}+1)). In the plane they are squares. We write 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} for the grid of dyadic squares of side rr, and Qn​(z)Q_{n}(z) for the unique level-nn cube containing zz. A dyadic parent or ancestor is a containing cube at a specified coarser level. A dyadic interval has the analogous one-dimensional meaning. For z≠0z\neq 0, arg⁡z\arg z denotes its angle modulo 2​π2\pi. An angular chart chooses a real representative on an arc shorter than a full circle. The notation A≲BA\lesssim B means A≤C​BA\leq CB with the stated parameters fixed, and A≳BA\gtrsim B means B≲AB\lesssim A, and A≍BA\asymp B or A∼BA\sim B means both inequalities. The notation A≪BA\ll B requires a sufficiently small ratio AB\frac{A}{B}, or a ratio tending to zero when a limit is specified. As usual, O⁡(B)O(B) denotes a quantity bounded in absolute value by C​BCB and o⁡(B)o(B) one whose ratio to BB tends to zero in the indicated limit. A loss δ−τ\delta^{-\tau}, where τ>0\tau>0 is fixed and small, is called a small power loss. It is distinguished from a fixed multiplicative constant, which does not change a dimension exponent.

We use the line-space metric defined in the introduction. In local coordinates, write a line as

Lθ,c={x∈ℝ2:(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)⋅x=c},L_{\theta,c}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\cdot x=c\},

where θ\theta is the angle of its unit normal and cc is its signed offset from the origin. If θ\theta ranges over a fixed interval of length less than π\pi and cc remains bounded, then

dist⁡(Lθ,c,Lθ′,c′)≍|θ−θ′|+|c−c′|.\operatorname{dist}(L_{\theta,c},L_{\theta^{\prime},c^{\prime}})\asymp|\theta-\theta^{\prime}|+|c-c^{\prime}|.

The comparison constants depend only on these parameter ranges. A ρ\rho-tube is a neighborhood of width C​ρC\rho of a line, with CC fixed. Tube separation means separation of their line parameters. A family of ρ\rho-tubes is parameter-separated if the defining lines of distinct members have line-space distance at least c​ρc\rho, where c>0c>0 is fixed. These conventions make the covering numbers of line families precise. Dyadic slope–intercept tubes used in the Ren–Wang estimate are introduced in Section 18. The overlap condition for the tubes and balls in the Fu–Gan–Ren estimate is given in Section 19.

Several letters are used with different meanings in different parts of the paper. We list them here, with the places where they are defined. The terminal resolution is δ=2−n\delta=2^{-n}, except in Lemma 23.2 and its proof, where δ<Δ\delta<\Delta are two auxiliary dyadic scales. In Part III, η\eta denotes the side length of the dyadic squares, called source parents, into which the source is grouped. In Section 23 it also denotes a small exponent loss. The dyadic scales ℓj\ell_{j} are used to classify the angular separations of source vertices about a pin. They determine the candidate widths ρj=δℓj\rho_{j}=\frac{\delta}{\ell_{j}} of the tubes about perpendicular bisectors. We write ρ\rho for the selected width (Sections 17 and 18). In the proof of Lemma 4.1, ℓj\ell_{j} instead denotes a precision. The pins are selected at resolution δ\delta and later thinned to resolution ρ\rho. The letters β,β0\beta,\beta_{0} denote deficits of lower envelopes in Sections C, 11 and 10, while in Part III the letter β\beta is the exponent loss in the source mass cap b=δλ−βb=\delta^{\lambda-\beta} (Section 17). The letter λ\lambda denotes the transfer level 1+Δ1+\Delta of Sections 8 and 11. Written without a set argument, Δ\Delta is this excess or the auxiliary scale above, never a distance set. The letters bb, kk, BB and QQ also have local meanings, fixed where they are introduced. We use ϱ\varrho for a distance value, such as |x−y||x-y|, in the finite-precision complexities defined below relative to the oracle (A,x)(A,x). The superscript AA denotes the fixed oracle. Scalar cutoffs such as A0A_{0} are local to the statements defining them. The constant η0\eta_{0} is reserved for the uniform gain in Theorem 1.2. The plateau parameters u−,u+,W,ς,χ,𝔢u_{-},u_{+},W,\varsigma,\chi,\mathfrak{e} are defined in Proposition 8.5. The subscripts in Hf,gH_{f,g} and H^f,g\widehat{H}_{f,g} identify the source profile ff and the pin profile gg, respectively (Sections 4 and 7).

2.2 Complexity at finite precision

Use the fixed universal prefix-free oracle machine UU of Section 1.3, with the usual optimality convention. Simulating another prefix-free machine adds at most a constant depending on that machine. The following are standard prefix-free complexity conventions [18]. Their finite-precision versions are as in [33, 7, §2]. Write {0,1}∗\{0,1\}^{*} for the set of finite binary strings. For finite binary strings σ,τ\sigma,\tau, the conditional prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity of σ\sigma given τ\tau is

K(σ∣τ)=min{|π|:π∈{0,1}∗,U(π,τ)=σ},K(\sigma\mid\tau)=\min\{|\pi|:\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*},\ U(\pi,\tau)=\sigma\},

the length of a shortest program that outputs σ\sigma when τ\tau is supplied as auxiliary input, and K⁡(σ)K(\sigma) is the same minimum with the empty string as auxiliary input. For an oracle A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N}, the quantities KA​(σ)K^{A}(\sigma) and KA​(σ∣τ)K^{A}(\sigma\mid\tau) are defined in the same way for a machine that may query membership in AA. Omitting the oracle superscript means that the oracle is empty. Rational points q∈ℚmq\in\mathbb{Q}^{m} are identified with their binary encodings under a fixed computable bijection, so that KA​(q)K^{A}(q) and KA​(p∣q)K^{A}(p\mid q) are defined. Thus the finite-precision complexity defined in the introduction is KrA​(z)=min⁡{KA​(q):q∈ℚm∩B⁡(z,2−r)}K_{r}^{A}(z)=\min\{K^{A}(q):q\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\cap B(z,2^{-r})\}. The convention K0A​(z)=0K_{0}^{A}(z)=0 is used only at the initial profile scale. The join A⊕BA\oplus B of two oracles encodes AA in the even positions and BB in the odd positions. A real point xx used as an oracle is encoded by the binary expansions of its coordinates, with terminating expansions chosen at dyadic rationals and with signs and integer parts included. Thus KA,xK^{A,x} uses the join of AA with this encoding and supplies arbitrarily precise rational approximations to xx. An oracle extends AA if it computes AA. Its set need not contain AA. For z∈ℝmz\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define finite conditioning by

Kr,sA​(z∣w)=maxq∈ℚn∩B⁡(w,2−s)⁡minp∈ℚm∩B⁡(z,2−r)​KA​(p∣q).K_{r,s}^{A}(z\mid w)=\max_{q\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}\cap B(w,2^{-s})}\min_{p\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\cap B(z,2^{-r})}K^{A}(p\mid q).

Equal-precision conditioning is abbreviated by KrA​(z∣w):=Kr,rA​(z∣w)K_{r}^{A}(z\mid w):=K_{r,r}^{A}(z\mid w). For conditioning points wi∈ℝniw_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}}, simultaneous finite conditioning means

KrA​(z∣w1,…,wk)=maxqi∈ℚni∩B⁡(wi,2−r)1≤i≤k⁡minp∈ℚm∩B⁡(z,2−r)​KA​(p∣⟨q1,…,qk⟩),K_{r}^{A}(z\mid w_{1},\ldots,w_{k})=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}q_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n_{i}}\cap B(w_{i},2^{-r})\\ 1\leq i\leq k\end{subarray}}\min_{p\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\cap B(z,2^{-r})}K^{A}(p\mid\langle q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\rangle),

where ⟨q1,…,qk⟩\langle q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\rangle is a fixed computable encoding of the ordered tuple as a finite string. The maximum makes this complexity a bound for every admissible collection of conditioning approximations. In contrast, real points in the oracle superscript supply all their binary digits. The quantity Kr,sA​(z∣z)K_{r,s}^{A}(z\mid z) is the number of bits needed to pass from precision ss to precision rr at the point zz. A dyadic square QQ is identified with the finite string that encodes its level and position. Thus KA​(Q)K^{A}(Q) is defined, and KnA​(z∣Q)K_{n}^{A}(z\mid Q) denotes the minimum of KA​(p∣Q)K^{A}(p\mid Q) over rational pp within 2−n2^{-n} of zz. Joins of several oracles, as in KA,G,xK^{A,G,x}, are formed in the same way as KA,xK^{A,x}. We use the standard finite-precision chain rules, symmetry of information, and oracle monotonicity (adding an oracle can only decrease a complexity, up to a fixed simulation cost). The notation KrA​(z,w)K_{r}^{A}(z,w) treats the pair as a point in the product Euclidean space. In particular, for fixed points and 1≤s≤r1\leq s\leq r, the chain rules used below include

KrA​(z,w)\displaystyle K_{r}^{A}(z,w) =KrA​(z)+KrA​(w∣z)+O⁡(log⁡r),\displaystyle=K_{r}^{A}(z)+K_{r}^{A}(w\mid z)+O(\log r),
Kr,sA​(z∣z)\displaystyle K_{r,s}^{A}(z\mid z) =KrA​(z)−KsA​(z)+O⁡(log⁡r).\displaystyle=K_{r}^{A}(z)-K_{s}^{A}(z)+O(\log r).

Interchanging z,wz,w in the first identity is the symmetry-of-information relation. The errors have the same order with any fixed additional oracles. See [33, 7, §2]. Finite conditioning on an approximation to a point is a weaker thing than full access to that point as an oracle, and we will need both.

The effective Hausdorff dimension of zz relative to AA is

dimAz=lim infr→∞KrA​(z)r.\dim^{A}z=\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A}(z)}{r}.

Its upper effective dimension, or effective packing dimension, is DimA⁡z=lim supr→∞KrA​(z)r\operatorname{Dim}^{A}z=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A}(z)}{r} [7, §2]. The same definitions apply to joined oracles. In particular,

dimA,xz=lim infr→∞KrA,x​(z)r,DimA,x⁡z=lim supr→∞KrA,x​(z)r.\dim^{A,x}z=\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A,x}(z)}{r},\qquad\operatorname{Dim}^{A,x}z=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A,x}(z)}{r}.

Here the machine has access to both AA and the full binary encoding of xx. The same convention applies to any finite list of additional oracles. A quantity is computable relative to AA if an oracle algorithm approximates it to every prescribed rational accuracy. It is lower semicomputable if such an algorithm produces an increasing rational sequence converging to it. A collection is computably enumerable relative to AA if an oracle algorithm lists its elements, with no requirement to decide nonmembership. The point-to-set principle [21] states that, for every F⊆ℝmF\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m},

dimHF=minA⊆ℕsupz∈FdimAz.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F=\min_{A\subseteq\mathbb{N}}\sup_{z\in F}\dim^{A}z.

A compact set F⊆ℝmF\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} is effectively compact relative to AA if the collection of finite families of rational open balls whose union covers FF is computably enumerable relative to AA. We also use the effectively compact form of the principle. If a compact set FF is effectively compact relative to AA, then dimHF=supz∈FdimAz\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F=\sup_{z\in F}\dim^{A}z. See [33, Theorem 5]. If FF is effectively compact relative to AA, then Δx​F\Delta_{x}F is effectively compact relative to (A,x)(A,x) [33, Proposition 7]. Compact sets and their measures are always encoded into the oracle before the points to which information estimates are applied are selected.

For a unit vector vv, write pv​z=z⋅vp_{v}z=z\cdot v. Effective projection estimates are developed in [22, 33, 7]. A nonintegral subscript of KK is rounded down to the nearest integer. A bounded change in precision changes complexity by at most O⁡(log⁡(r+2))O(\log(r+2)) at terminal precision rr. The convention at precision zero is as above.

2.3 The pointwise hypotheses

For fixed distinct points x,yx,y, put 𝐞=y−x|y−x|\mathbf{e}=\frac{y-x}{|y-x|}. The pointwise hypotheses are the conditions of [7, §4] for both choices of pin.

  1. (H1)

    dimAx>1\dim^{A}x>1 and dimAy>1\dim^{A}y>1.

  2. (H2)

    KrA,x​(𝐞)≥r−O⁡(log⁡r)K_{r}^{A,x}(\mathbf{e})\geq r-O(\log r) and KrA,y​(𝐞)≥r−O⁡(log⁡r)K_{r}^{A,y}(\mathbf{e})\geq r-O(\log r).

  3. (H3)

    KrA,x​(y)≥KrA​(y)−O⁡(log⁡r)K_{r}^{A,x}(y)\geq K_{r}^{A}(y)-O(\log r) and KrA,y​(x)≥KrA​(x)−O⁡(log⁡r)K_{r}^{A,y}(x)\geq K_{r}^{A}(x)-O(\log r).

  4. (H4)

    KrA​(𝐞∣x)≥r−o⁡(r)K_{r}^{A}(\mathbf{e}\mid x)\geq r-o(r) and KrA​(𝐞∣y)≥r−o⁡(r)K_{r}^{A}(\mathbf{e}\mid y)\geq r-o(r). These finite-precision bounds follow from (H2), up to logarithmic precision costs.

The constants may depend on the fixed pair and base oracle. The directional complexity deficiency at precision rr relative to (A,x)(A,x) means r−KrA,x​(𝐞)r-K_{r}^{A,x}(\mathbf{e}). Thus (H2) says that this quantity is at most logarithmic in rr. This is the directional randomness referred to below. Condition (H3) is the full-oracle independence condition. Supplying the other endpoint saves at most logarithmically many bits.

To obtain the bound Y⁡(dimHE)Y(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E) in (1.1), where YY and S0S_{0} are defined in Theorem 1.2, we prove the following pointwise estimate. Let 0≤κ<κ0:=S0−10\leq\kappa<\kappa_{0}:=S_{0}-1. If x,yx,y satisfy (H1)–(H4) and dimAx,dimAy>1+κ\dim^{A}x,\dim^{A}y>1+\kappa, then

lim infr→∞KrA​(|x−y|)r≥Y⁡(1+κ).\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A}(|x-y|)}{r}\geq Y(1+\kappa). (2.1)

Here KrA​(|x−y|)K_{r}^{A}(|x-y|) is computed using only the background oracle AA, with neither xx nor yy supplied as an additional oracle. Supplying either endpoint can only shorten a description, up to a fixed simulation cost. Consequently

max⁡{KrA,x​(|x−y|),KrA,y​(|x−y|)}≤KrA​(|x−y|)+O⁡(1).\max\{K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|),K_{r}^{A,y}(|x-y|)\}\leq K_{r}^{A}(|x-y|)+O(1). (2.2)

Thus KrA​(|x−y|)K_{r}^{A}(|x-y|) bounds both pin-conditioned distance complexities from above, up to a fixed additive constant. Which of these two conditioned complexities is larger may depend on the precision. Our unpinned argument allows this dependence. It does not require the same choice of pin to give the stronger lower bound at every scale.

2.4 Information profiles and the two choices of pin

A point in a bounded part of the plane has KrA​(z)≤2​r+O⁡(log⁡r)K_{r}^{A}(z)\leq 2r+O(\log r). More generally, increasing the precision from mm to nn costs at most 2​(n−m)+O​(log⁡n)2(n-m)+O(\log n) bits. These bounds allow us to retain the information at intermediate scales, as follows.

Fix A,x,yA,x,y satisfying the pointwise hypotheses and a sequence rj→∞r_{j}\to\infty. The four normalized functions used to define f,g,dx,dyf,g,d_{x},d_{y} in Section 1.3 have a common subsequence converging uniformly on [0,1][0,1]. The initial value is zero, and logarithmic errors disappear after division by rjr_{j}. The endpoint profiles are nondecreasing and 22-Lipschitz, and

u≤f⁡(u),g⁡(u)≤2​ufor ​0≤u≤1.u\leq f(u),\,g(u)\leq 2u\qquad\text{for }0\leq u\leq 1. (2.3)

The distance profiles are nondecreasing and 11-Lipschitz. In particular 0≤dx​(u),dy​(u)≤u0\leq d_{x}(u),d_{y}(u)\leq u. When these functions are considered only through their displayed inequalities, without requiring a realization by points, we refer to them as scalar profiles. The compactness assertion follows from the preceding precision increment bounds by linear interpolation and the usual uniform compactness argument for functions with a common Lipschitz bound, allowing errors tending to zero.

Lemma 2.1 (Joint extraction).

Every sequence of terminal precisions tending to infinity has one subsequence along which the four profiles f,g,dx,dyf,g,d_{x},d_{y} above converge uniformly. Along that same subsequence, the prefix and interval-transfer inequalities hold for both choices of pin.

Proof.

Apply the compactness argument just given to the four functions successively, retaining each preceding convergence. Lemma 3.1 holds at every precision, and Lemma 4.1 holds along every subsequence on which the profiles converge, so both conclusions hold along this one. ∎

Table 2 records how the profiles are relabelled when the endpoints exchange roles.

By (2.2), an upper bound for KrA​(|x−y|)K_{r}^{A}(|x-y|) controls both distance profiles. For a prescribed pin only dxd_{x} is controlled, so the unpinned argument cannot be used without change. Throughout the paper the points and oracle are chosen before the precision varies.

In the arguments below, we partition intervals of precision scales into smaller intervals. Let FF denote either a complexity function, extended to real precision by linear interpolation between successive precision levels, or a limiting profile. Put h⁡(u)=F⁡(u)−uh(u)=F(u)-u. Thus

h⁡(b)−h⁡(a)=F⁡(b)−F⁡(a)−(b−a)h(b)-h(a)=F(b)-F(a)-(b-a)

measures the growth of FF on [a,b][a,b] relative to growth at rate one.

Following the color conventions of [33, §3] and [7, §§3–4], we call an interval [a,b][a,b]:

  • •

    yellow if hh attains its minimum at the left endpoint: h⁡(u)≥h⁡(a)h(u)\geq h(a) for every u∈[a,b]u\in[a,b];

  • •

    teal if hh attains its minimum at the right endpoint: h⁡(u)≥h⁡(b)h(u)\geq h(b) for every u∈[a,b]u\in[a,b];

  • •

    green if both conditions hold: h⁡(a)=h⁡(b)=minu∈[a,b]⁡h⁡(u)h(a)=h(b)=\min_{u\in[a,b]}h(u).

These conditions specify where the minimum is attained. They do not require hh to be monotone. In particular, a green interval need not be an interval on which hh is constant.

A labelled yellow–teal partition assigns each interval one of the labels yellow or teal, according to the conditions above. A green interval may receive either label. The yellow loss is

∑[a,b]​ in the partition[a,b]​ labelled yellow(h⁡(b)−h⁡(a)).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}[a,b]\text{ in the partition}\\ [a,b]\text{ labelled yellow}\end{subarray}}\bigl(h(b)-h(a)\bigr).

Every summand is nonnegative, and green intervals contribute zero.

For the auxiliary piecewise linear constructions, we also call a piece red when hh is increasing on it and blue when hh is decreasing on it. A red–green–blue sequence consists of pieces with these colors occurring in that order as the precision increases. In each application, the partition intervals must also satisfy the length restrictions stated there.

2.5 From dyadic masses to descriptions

The following elementary coding fact will be used both in the geometric reduction and in the optional application in the appendix. A measure is computable relative to AA here when its dyadic masses can be approximated by oracle programs with any prescribed rational error.

Lemma 2.2 (Coding a computable measure).

Let A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N} be an oracle, and let μ\mu be a compactly supported probability measure on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} whose dyadic masses are uniformly computable relative to AA. That is, a single algorithm with access to AA, given a dyadic square QQ and an integer m≥1m\geq 1, approximates μ⁡(Q)\mu(Q) with error at most 2−m2^{-m}.

Then, for μ\mu-almost every zz,

KnA​(z)=−log2⁡μ⁡(Qn​(z))+Oz​(log⁡(n+2)).K_{n}^{A}(z)=-\log_{2}\mu(Q_{n}(z))+O_{z}(\log(n+2)). (2.4)

Moreover, for each fixed oracle BB such that AA is computable relative to BB, one has

KnB​(z)≥−log2⁡μ⁡(Qn​(z))−OB,z​(log⁡(n+2))K_{n}^{B}(z)\geq-\log_{2}\mu(Q_{n}(z))-O_{B,z}(\log(n+2))

for μ\mu-almost every zz. The exceptional null set may depend on BB.

In particular, for each fixed x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

KnA,x​(y)≥KnA​(y)−Ox,y​(log⁡(n+2))K_{n}^{A,x}(y)\geq K_{n}^{A}(y)-O_{x,y}(\log(n+2))

for μ\mu-almost every yy, with an exceptional null set that may depend on xx.

Proof.

Kraft’s inequality states that a prefix-free set of binary strings ww satisfies ∑w2−|w|≤1\sum_{w}2^{-|w|}\leq 1, and conversely that lengths ℓi\ell_{i} with ∑i2−ℓi≤1\sum_{i}2^{-\ell_{i}}\leq 1 are the codeword lengths of a prefix-free code [4, Chapter 5]. We use its effective form, the Kraft–Chaitin theorem [18, Chapter 4], as follows. Given nn, for each level-nn square QQ and integer k≥0k\geq 0, request a codeword of length k+1k+1 for QQ once a rational mass approximation proves μ⁡(Q)>2−k\mu(Q)>2^{-k}. Each request is made once. These requests can be enumerated relative to AA, and

∑Q∑k:2−k<μ⁡(Q)2−(k+1)≤∑Qμ(Q)=1.\sum_{Q}\sum_{k:2^{-k}<\mu(Q)}2^{-(k+1)}\leq\sum_{Q}\mu(Q)=1.

For every square of positive mass the shortest requested length is at most −log2⁡μ⁡(Q)+2-\log_{2}\mu(Q)+2. The theorem therefore produces a prefix-free code with this bound by one procedure relative to AA taking nn as input. This avoids having to decide whether a computable mass equals a dyadic threshold. Given the level nn and a codeword assigned to a square QQ, the decoding algorithm, with access to AA, outputs the label of QQ. Thus the codeword, together with a description of nn, provides a description of the square. Since describing nn costs O⁡(log⁡(n+2))O(\log(n+2)) bits, we obtain

KA​(Qn​(z))≤−log2⁡μ⁡(Qn​(z))+O⁡(log⁡(n+2)).K^{A}(Q_{n}(z))\leq-\log_{2}\mu(Q_{n}(z))+O(\log(n+2)).

For the reverse inequality, the shortest programs of distinct level-nn squares relative to BB form a prefix-free set, so the direct form of Kraft’s inequality implies ∑Q2−KB​(Q)≤1\sum_{Q}2^{-K^{B}(Q)}\leq 1. Every square in the set below has μ⁡(Q)<(n+2)−4​2−KB​(Q)\mu(Q)<(n+2)^{-4}2^{-K^{B}(Q)}, hence, for each fixed BB,

μ⁡{z∈ℝ2:KB​(Qn​(z))<−log2⁡μ⁡(Qn​(z))−4​log2⁡(n+2)}≤(n+2)−4.\mu\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:K^{B}(Q_{n}(z))<-\log_{2}\mu(Q_{n}(z))-4\log_{2}(n+2)\}\leq(n+2)^{-4}.

The sum of these upper bounds is finite. The Borel–Cantelli lemma therefore says that almost every zz belongs to only finitely many of the displayed exceptional sets, proving the reverse bound. A precision-nn approximation to zz identifies Qn​(z)Q_{n}(z) among a bounded number of squares. Conversely, the label of Qn​(z)Q_{n}(z) together with an index among its fixed-depth descendants specifies a center within 2−n2^{-n} of zz. The index has bounded length. It need not be determined by the square alone. Thus point and square complexities differ by O⁡(log⁡(n+2))O(\log(n+2)). This proves both assertions. The last follows by taking B=(A,x)B=(A,x) and using the first assertion. The exceptional null set may depend on BB. In particular, we do not intersect the full-measure sets over all real pins. We first fix a pin, apply the almost-everywhere assertion in the source variable, and then use Fubini for the two fixed measures. ∎

Part I Information at the two endpoints

3   Retaining information in the projection estimates

We derive the estimates below by retaining intermediate complexity quantities in the arguments of Stull and Fiedler–Stull. One involves the source, and the other involves the pin. Keeping these quantities allows the two endpoint profiles to interact. We identify the relevant inequalities in the earlier proofs and check uniformity in the projection direction. Appendix A gives the source-increment summation and the modifications needed at upper effective dimension two. Directional uniformity matters because, in Section 4, that direction is determined by a competitor, a point zz at the same distance from the pin as yy, which a short description of the distance cannot distinguish from yy.

Lemma 3.1 (Prefix estimate).

Under (H1)–(H4), with xx as the pin,

KrA,x​(|x−y|)≥r2+14​KrA​(y)−o⁡(r).K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|)\geq\frac{r}{2}+\frac{1}{4}K_{r}^{A}(y)-o(r). (3.1)

The same bound holds with xx and yy exchanged.

Proof.

The argument of [7, §4.3] partitions the range of precisions [1,r][1,r] into blocks of two kinds, called yellow and teal. On a yellow block the complexity of the distance grows at least as fast as the precision, and on a teal block it grows at least as fast as the complexity of the source. Let LrL_{r} be the total length of the yellow blocks. Proposition A.2, proved in Appendix A, establishes, for this LrL_{r}, the two retained inequalities

KrA,x​(|x−y|)≥2​r+Lr3−o⁡(r),KrA,x​(|x−y|)≥KrA​(y)−Lr−o⁡(r).K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|)\geq\frac{2r+L_{r}}{3}-o(r),\qquad K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|)\geq K_{r}^{A}(y)-L_{r}-o(r).

Their weighted average with coefficients 34\frac{3}{4} and 14\frac{1}{4} is the asserted bound. The appendix constructs the partition, proves the transfer on its teal blocks at D=2D=2, and sums the errors before removing the pin from the source complexity. ∎

The point of retaining the source complexity is visible in the weighted average because the unknown yellow length cancels exactly.

34​2​r+L3+14​(KrA​(y)−L)=r2+KrA​(y)4.\frac{3}{4}\frac{2r+L}{3}+\frac{1}{4}(K_{r}^{A}(y)-L)=\frac{r}{2}+\frac{K_{r}^{A}(y)}{4}.

The second borrowed estimate is Stull’s projection theorem, read so as to keep the terminal complexity of the projected point. Here KRA​(x∣pv​x,v)K_{R}^{A}(x\mid p_{v}x,v) uses precision-RR rational approximations to both pv​x=x⋅vp_{v}x=x\cdot v and vv as finite auxiliary input, taking the worst case over these approximations as in Section 2.2. The background oracle is AA.

Lemma 3.2 (Projection estimate retaining terminal complexity).

Let xx satisfy dimAx>1\dim^{A}x>1. Fix τ>0\tau>0. Suppose τ​R≤t≤R\tau R\leq t\leq R and v∈S1v\in S^{1} satisfies

KsA,x​(v)≥s−C​log⁡R for ​1≤s≤tK_{s}^{A,x}(v)\geq s-C\log R\quad\text{ for }1\leq s\leq t

with a fixed constant CC. This is the directional-randomness input in [33, Theorem 13], in its local uniform form. Then

KRA​(x∣pv​x,v)≤max⁡{KRA​(x)−R,KRA​(x)−t2}+o⁡(R).K_{R}^{A}(x\mid p_{v}x,v)\leq\max\left\{K_{R}^{A}(x)-R,\frac{K_{R}^{A}(x)-t}{2}\right\}+o(R). (3.2)

min⁡{R,KRA​(x)+t2}−o⁡(R).\min\left\{R,\frac{K_{R}^{A}(x)+t}{2}\right\}-o(R). (3.3)

KRA​(x∣pv​x,v)≤KRA​(x)−R+o⁡(R).K_{R}^{A}(x\mid p_{v}x,v)\leq K_{R}^{A}(x)-R+o(R).

There is one endpoint issue to address before using these estimates. In [7], the parameter DD bounds the upper effective dimensions of the two points. 4   The interval transfer lemma

Suppose the distance from yy to xx is known, as is a coarse approximation to yy. How many further bits are needed to locate yy accurately? A competitor zz must lie near that coarse location and on the same circle about xx. If every such competitor requires a long description, a short description of the distance cannot hide much source information. This is the transfer principle used by Stull and Fiedler–Stull.

We retain the dependence on |z−y||z-y|. This separation determines the precision at which the competitor reveals a projection of the pin, and hence the part of the pin profile that enters the estimate.

Suppose |x−z|=|x−y||x-z|=|x-y| and s=−log2⁡|y−z|s=-\log_{2}|y-z|. We consider 0<s≤r0<s\leq r, the separation range required by the transfer lemma below. The exact identity

|𝐞⋅y−z|y−z||=|y−z|2​|x−y|\left|\mathbf{e}\cdot\frac{y-z}{|y-z|}\right|=\frac{|y-z|}{2|x-y|}

shows that the unit normal v=y−z|y−z|v=\frac{y-z}{|y-z|} to the perpendicular bisector lies within Cx,y​2−sC_{x,y}2^{-s} of one of the two perpendiculars to 𝐞\mathbf{e}. The sign costs at most one bit. Thus (H2) supplies a common logarithmic directional-deficiency bound through precision s−c0s-c_{0}, where c0c_{0} depends only on the fixed pair.

The equal-distance condition also places xx on the perpendicular bisector of [y,z][y,z]. Consequently,

pv​x=pv​(y+z2)=|y|2−|z|22​|y−z|.p_{v}x=p_{v}\left(\frac{y+z}{2}\right)=\frac{|y|^{2}-|z|^{2}}{2|y-z|}.

The complexity bound below combines two contributions. The term KsA​(y)K_{s}^{A}(y) accounts for the coarse position information shared by yy and zz. The minimum term accounts for the additional information about the pin revealed by the perpendicular-bisector constraint, using Lemma 3.2 at precision r−sr-s and the directional bound established above. KrA​(z)≥KsA​(y)+min⁡{r−s,Kr−sA​(x)+s2}−o⁡(r).K_{r}^{A}(z)\geq K_{s}^{A}(y)+\min\left\{r-s,\frac{K_{r-s}^{A}(x)+s}{2}\right\}-o(r). (4.1)

The transfer argument uses an auxiliary device from [7, Lemma 14]. The geometric and information-theoretic input is now contained in three groups of inequalities: the profile bounds (2.3), the prefix estimates (4.2), and the interval transfers (4.5). The next section shows how to choose a fixed pair satisfying these hypotheses. The elementary consequences in Appendices B and C give a short introduction to the scalar argument. The stronger estimates are proved in Sections 11 and 10.

5   From a pair of points to a set

The scalar inequalities concern one fixed pair of points. To use it for a distance set, we must choose a pair that has enough complexity and enough independence in both directions. The point-to-set principle requires this for every initial oracle. We first enlarge that oracle to include the fixed geometric data, and only then choose the pair. All precisions will use this same choice.

For a compact set, we can encode a sequence of finite rational sets whose Hausdorff distances from it are at most 2−j2^{-j} at stage jj. This supplies approximations with a known error, and makes the compact set effectively compact relative to the encoding oracle. For a finite measure, enumerate the dyadic cubes and encode rational approximations to every cube mass, each with error at most 2−j2^{-j} at stage jj. Include the total mass and a bound for the support. These are countably many finite strings, so a fixed coding of finite strings and indices places all the data in one oracle A0A_{0}. Positive total masses can then be divided out to compute the normalized measures. The coordinate boundaries have measure zero for the measures used below, since their Frostman exponents exceed one.

Given an arbitrary oracle BB, use the join A=B⊕A0A=B\oplus A_{0}: even positions encode BB and odd positions encode A0A_{0}. Thus a computation with oracle AA has access to all the fixed geometric data and can simulate a computation with oracle BB. No effective procedure for constructing A0A_{0} from an arbitrary analytic set is required. The point-to-set principle permits every oracle, and the data are fixed before any point is selected.

Proposition 5.1 (A fixed pair for every oracle).

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be analytic with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1, and let 1<s<dimHE1<s<\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E. For every oracle BB there are an oracle A=B⊕A0A=B\oplus A_{0} and points x,y∈Ex,y\in E satisfying (H1)–(H4) relative to AA, with dimAx≥s\dim^{A}x\geq s and dimAy≥s\dim^{A}y\geq s.

Proof.

Choose separated compact pieces E1,E2⊂EE_{1},E_{2}\subset E with positive finite ss-dimensional Hausdorff measure. By the Hausdorff density theorem [23, Theorem 6.2], the upper ss-density of ℋs|Ei\mathcal{H}^{s}|_{E_{i}} is finite almost everywhere. A countable restriction followed by inner regularity provides compact positive-measure subsets Ei′⊂EiE_{i}^{\prime}\subset E_{i} and common constants C,r0>0C,r_{0}>0 such that ℋs​(Ei∩B⁡(z,r))≤C​rs\mathcal{H}^{s}(E_{i}\cap B(z,r))\leq Cr^{s} for z∈Ei′z\in E_{i}^{\prime} and 0<r<r00<r<r_{0}. If B⁡(w,r)B(w,r) meets Ei′E_{i}^{\prime} at zz, it lies in B⁡(z,2​r)B(z,2r). Enlarging CC for r≥r02r\geq\frac{r_{0}}{2} proves that ℋs|Ei′\mathcal{H}^{s}|_{E_{i}^{\prime}} is ss-Frostman. Let μi\mu_{i} be its normalization and fix 1<t<s1<t<s. Both measures have finite tt-energy.

Start with an arbitrary oracle BB, and use the preceding construction to form A=B⊕A0A=B\oplus A_{0}, encoding both compact pieces, their finite Hausdorff restrictions, the total masses, and all dyadic cell masses. This supplies the hypotheses of [33, Lemma 36(2)], also after normalization. For each fixed endpoint xx, that lemma establishes full-oracle independence for almost every opposite endpoint yy. Apply it for both choices of pin and then use Fubini to obtain (H3) for product-almost every pair. For every fixed AA, the set {z∈ℝ2:dimAz<s}\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim^{A}z<s\} has zero ℋs\mathcal{H}^{s} measure by the usual low-complexity covers. Thus (H1) also holds almost everywhere, even though the background oracle contains the measure data.

Orponen’s radial absolute-continuity theorem [25, Theorem 1.11] has an exceptional pin set of dimension at most 2−t<12-t<1. The opposite ss-dimensional measure assigns this set zero mass. For each fixed pin, the angular complexity deficiency set relative to that pin and AA has zero arclength by [33, Lemma 36(1)]. Radial absolute continuity and Fubini give (H2) for product-almost every pair, with either endpoint as the pin. The bad-pair relations here are Borel because the finite-precision oracle computation conditions are countable combinations of finite-query conditions. The finite conditional directional conditions follow directly from the full-oracle bounds. Fix one pair in the intersection of these full-measure sets.

The pair satisfies dimAx,dimAy≥s\dim^{A}x,\dim^{A}y\geq s, since the set {z∈ℝ2:dimAz<s}\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\dim^{A}z<s\} is ℋs\mathcal{H}^{s}-null. Thus the quantifier order is

∀B​∃A=B⊕A0​∃(x,y)∈E1×E2\displaystyle\forall B\,\exists A=B\oplus A_{0}\,\exists(x,y)\in E_{1}\times E_{2}
∀ sufficiently large precisions, with (H1)–(H4) satisfied by this same pair.\displaystyle\forall\text{ sufficiently large precisions, with (H1)--(H4) satisfied by this same pair. }

Choosing different pairs at different scales would not suffice. The scalar bounds for this pair, YY and the scalar bound 45\frac{4}{5}, are proved in Sections 11 and 10, after the partition estimates of Part II. Together with the point-to-set principle they prove Theorem 1.2. The term R⁡(dimHE)R(\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E) follows from Theorem 1.5. ∎

There is no pinned conclusion from this argument alone. A low unconditioned distance complexity forces both endpoint-conditioned complexities to be low simultaneously. A low complexity conditioned on the prescribed pin xx alone does not provide (B.2), whose derivation used the upper bound for the distance complexity conditioned on yy. Part II identifies the resulting scalar obstruction and the critical profile structure used in the geometric proof.

6   The asymmetric pinned refinement

What can the information estimates prove when the pin is prescribed? We first separate the lower dimension of the pin from that of the source. Fiedler and Stull use one parameter for both, and note in their footnote 7 that this restriction can be relaxed. Keeping the two parameters separate yields an explicit exceptional-set estimate. The proof uses the partition argument alone.
