Part II Partition estimates and the two endpoint profiles

7   Why the scalar method stops at three quarters

The estimates just proved still approach 34\frac{3}{4} as the source dimension decreases to one. Is this only a weakness in how we optimized them? The following construction shows that it is a limitation of the pointwise scalar system without a common-source mass bound. The later annular cap records information about one measure across many pairs, which is an additional kind of constraint.

We allow every finite yellow–teal partition from Stull’s projection argument, so the obstruction persists even after the projection gain is strengthened. The resulting profiles satisfy all the displayed inequalities, have endpoint dimensions greater than one, and have dx​(1)d_{x}(1) arbitrarily close to 34\frac{3}{4}. The opposite distance profile has dy​(1)=1d_{y}(1)=1, which explains why the unpinned argument leads to no contradiction.

The stronger partition functional has a second use. Near the barrier, it forces the pin profile to contain a plateau. That plateau will provide the pin spacing estimates in Part III.

For a profile gg, put hg​(u)=g⁡(u)−uh_{g}(u)=g(u)-u. For a labelled yellow–teal partition 𝒫\mathcal{P}, define its loss by

lossg⁡(𝒫)=∑[v,w]∈𝒫​ yellow(hg​(w)−hg​(v)).\operatorname{loss}_{g}(\mathcal{P})=\sum_{[v,w]\in\mathcal{P}\text{ yellow}}\bigl(h_{g}(w)-h_{g}(v)\bigr).

Let ℒt​(g,R)\mathcal{L}_{t}(g;R) be the infimum of this loss over finite partitions of [0,R][0,R] with piece lengths at most tt. The colors have the endpoint-minimum meanings given in Section 2.4. A partition template records its ordered endpoints and color labels. It can be transported to a nearby interval as in the next lemma. Define

Pg​(t,R)=g⁡(R)−ℒt​(g,R),p^g​(t,b)=max⁡{min⁡{b−t,g⁡(b−t)+t2},Pg​(t,b−t)},P_{g}(t;R)=g(R)-\mathcal{L}_{t}(g;R),\qquad\widehat{p}_{g}(t;b)=\max\left\{\min\left\{b-t,\frac{g(b-t)+t}{2}\right\},P_{g}(t;b-t)\right\},

and set Pg​(t,0)=0P_{g}(t;0)=0, so p^g​(b,b)=0\widehat{p}_{g}(b;b)=0. For 0<a≤b≤10<a\leq b\leq 1, define

H^f,g​(a,b)=min⁡{f⁡(b),infa≤t≤b(f⁡(t)+p^g​(t,b))}.\widehat{H}_{f,g}(a,b)=\min\left\{f(b),\inf_{a\leq t\leq b}\bigl(f(t)+\widehat{p}_{g}(t;b)\bigr)\right\}.

Thus H^f,g\widehat{H}_{f,g} is Hf,gH_{f,g} with pgp_{g} replaced by p^g\widehat{p}_{g}. Telescoping the increments of hgh_{g} shows that ℒt​(g,R)≥hg​(R)\mathcal{L}_{t}(g;R)\geq h_{g}(R), because teal increments are nonpositive. Consequently

p^g​(t,b)≤b−t.\widehat{p}_{g}(t;b)\leq b-t. (7.1)

Lemma 8.3 below shows that Pg​(t,b−t)≥pg​(t,b)P_{g}(t;b-t)\geq p_{g}(t;b), so in fact p^g​(t,b)=Pg​(t,b−t)\widehat{p}_{g}(t;b)=P_{g}(t;b-t) for t<bt<b. We keep the closed gain in the notation because pgp_{g}, unlike PgP_{g} (Remark 7.4), is monotone in gg, which the envelope arguments of Sections B, C, and 11 use.

Lemma 7.1 (Uniform finite witnesses for the partition gain).

The map (g,t,R)↦Pg​(t,R)(g,t,R)\mapsto P_{g}(t;R) is lower semicontinuous for the uniform topology on profiles and for t,R>0t,R>0. There exist ξ>0\xi>0, an integer mm, and finitely many finite partition templates with the following property. If ‖f′−f‖∞+‖g′−g‖∞<ξ\|f^{\prime}-f\|_{\infty}+\|g^{\prime}-g\|_{\infty}<\xi, then f′​(b)>c+ξf^{\prime}(b)>c+\xi and, for every t∈[a,b2]t\in[a,\frac{b}{2}], either the closed projection gain or a partition obtained from one of the templates yields

The partition 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} has at most mm pieces, covers [0,b−t][0,b-t], and has all piece lengths at most tt. Templates are transported by linear rescaling, trimming, and splitting at minima. Thus the number of pieces and the strict margin are uniform in the competitor separation.

Proof.

Put h=g−uh=g-u. Take a witnessing partition of [0,R][0,R] with kk pieces and loss BB. If (R′,t′,g′)(R^{\prime},t^{\prime},g^{\prime}) is close to (R,t,g)(R,t,g), rescale its endpoints by R′R\frac{R^{\prime}}{R}. The transported function and h′=g′−uh^{\prime}=g^{\prime}-u differ by at most

on corresponding points. Split each transported piece at a minimum of h′h^{\prime}. For an originally yellow piece, its new loss is at most its old loss plus twice this error. For an originally teal piece the new loss is at most twice this error. Indeed, if vv is the new minimum on [u,w][u,w], the repaired loss is h′​(w)−h′​(v)h^{\prime}(w)-h^{\prime}(v).

A transported piece exceeds t′t^{\prime} by at most e=tR​|R′−R|+|t′−t|e=\frac{t}{R}|R^{\prime}-R|+|t^{\prime}-t|. In a sufficiently small neighborhood e<t′e<t^{\prime}. For a yellow piece, split off its terminal excess and repair that short piece at a minimum. For a teal piece, keep its terminal interval of length t′t^{\prime} and repair the short initial piece. The 11-Lipschitz bound charges at most 2​e2e per piece. Hence a repaired partition has at most 6​k6k pieces and loss

B+Ok,R,t​(‖g′−g‖∞+|R′−R|+|t′−t|).B+O_{k,R,t}\bigl(\|g^{\prime}-g\|_{\infty}+|R^{\prime}-R|+|t^{\prime}-t|\bigr).

Now put ηgap=H^f,g​(a,b)−c>0\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}=\widehat{H}_{f,g}(a,b)-c>0. At every t∈[a,b2]t\in[a,\frac{b}{2}], the closed gain or one finite partition witnesses a sum greater than c+3​ηgap4c+\frac{3\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}}{4}. The terminal cap satisfies f⁡(b)≥c+ηgapf(b)\geq c+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}. Lemma 7.2 (The full partition transfer).

Let x,yx,y satisfy (H1)–(H4) relative to AA. Along every sequence of precisions on which the four profiles converge uniformly, the limiting profiles satisfy

dx​(b)−dx​(a)≥[H^f,g​(a,b)−f⁡(a)]+for ​0<a<b≤1,d_{x}(b)-d_{x}(a)\geq[\widehat{H}_{f,g}(a,b)-f(a)]_{+}\quad\text{for }0<a<b\leq 1,

and, with yy as the pin,

dy​(b)−dy​(a)≥[H^g,f​(a,b)−g⁡(a)]+.d_{y}(b)-d_{y}(a)\geq[\widehat{H}_{g,f}(a,b)-g(a)]_{+}.
Proof.

Fix a finite yellow–teal partition of [0,R][0,R] with interval lengths at most tt. Uniform convergence of the normalized pin complexity makes its intervals approximately yellow or teal, with errors tending to zero. The hypotheses in [33, Lemmas 14–15] already allow an additive error proportional to the terminal precision of the interval. If the uniform profile error is εN→0\varepsilon_{N}\to 0, the yellow or teal condition has slack at most 2​εN​N+O⁡(log⁡N)2\varepsilon_{N}N+O(\log N) after rounding and applying the chain rule. On pieces whose terminal precision is at least κ​N\kappa N, this slack is o⁡(1)o(1) times that precision, for each fixed κ>0\kappa>0. Thus those lemmas apply. A yellow interval costs its increment of g−ug-u, and a teal interval costs o⁡(1)o(1) after normalization. The chain rule sums these costs over the fixed finite partition, as in [33, Lemma 17]. Directional randomness through t​N−O⁡(log⁡N)tN-O(\log N) suffices. At a length boundary, trim an O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) precision segment from the right endpoint of a yellow interval or the left endpoint of a teal interval, preserving its color condition, and charge the removed segment by its full complexity. Thus this partition retains g⁡(R)g(R) minus its yellow loss. Take the infimum over finite partitions after the large-precision limit. No effective procedure for recovering a limiting profile or an optimal partition is needed. Once the cap and its strict margin are fixed, the next paragraph selects finitely many templates with a fixed bound on their numbers of pieces. At precision NN, encode their rounded integer endpoints and color labels as part of the description. This costs O⁡(m​log⁡(N+2))O(m\log(N+2)) bits for at most mm pieces, and hence disappears after division by NN. The template count is fixed before NN tends to infinity.

Lemma 7.1 supplies finitely many partition templates and a uniform strict margin for a cap below H^f,g​(a,b)\widehat{H}_{f,g}(a,b) on the early separation interval [a,b2][a,\frac{b}{2}]. If that interval is empty, only the tangent estimate is needed. To avoid any threshold issue from tiny pieces, discard an initial precision range [0,κ​N][0,\kappa N], costing at most 2​κ​N+o⁡(N)2\kappa N+o(N), and charge newly trimmed tiny pieces by their full complexity. Hold κ>0\kappa>0 fixed as N→∞N\to\infty, then let κ↘0\kappa\searrow 0. Every remaining local projection estimate is applied at a uniformly positive macroscopic precision. The direction-uniform bounds in [33, Lemmas 14–15] therefore apply to all competitors.

For t≥b2t\geq\frac{b}{2}, the tangent estimate yields b−tb-t as before. Substituting these uniform projection bounds into the capped collision argument of Lemma 4.1 completes the proof. The positive pin information is preserved by the lowering oracle and its negative projection residual can only decrease. No randomness relative to that extra oracle is assumed. ∎

Remark 7.4 (The partition gain is not monotone).

Let g1​(u)=ug_{1}(u)=u and g2​(u)=u+h0​(u)g_{2}(u)=u+h_{0}(u), with h0h_{0} as in the preceding proof. Then g1≤g2g_{1}\leq g_{2}, but

Pg1​(14,34)=34,Pg2​(14,34)=12.P_{g_{1}}\left(\frac{1}{4};\frac{3}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{4},\qquad P_{g_{2}}\left(\frac{1}{4};\frac{3}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.

For g1g_{1}, every partition has zero loss. For g2g_{2}, a partition piece of length at most 14\frac{1}{4} meeting the initial increase in a positive-length interval ends before 12\frac{1}{2} and cannot be teal. The yellow costs therefore sum to at least 14\frac{1}{4}. The partition with endpoints 0,14,12,340,\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4} attains that loss. Thus a pointwise pin lower envelope cannot be substituted inside PgP_{g}. The envelope updates in Sections B and C use only the closed gain pgp_{g}. The plateau argument below and the proof of Theorem 1.2 in Section 11 work directly with partition losses.

An affine pin profile g⁡(u)=σ​ug(u)=\sigma u, 1≤σ≤21\leq\sigma\leq 2, illustrates the information recovered by the full partition gain. Its loss is (σ−1)​R(\sigma-1)R for every partition, so Pg​(t,R)=RP_{g}(t;R)=R. The full transfer then implies H^f,g​(a,1)≥1\widehat{H}_{f,g}(a,1)\geq 1, since f⁡(u)≥uf(u)\geq u. Consequently dx​(1)≥1−f⁡(a)≥1−2​ad_{x}(1)\geq 1-f(a)\geq 1-2a for every a>0a>0, and dx​(1)=1d_{x}(1)=1 follows by letting aa tend to zero.

The countermodel is a statement about the displayed pointwise inequalities, without the common-source mass bound of Proposition 14.2. It does not assert that a Euclidean pair realizes all four profiles. The next section derives the common structure of nearly critical profiles. The geometric argument will use information shared by several actual pairs.

8   The plateau forced by a small pinned distance profile

The scalar obstruction does more than explain the limitation of the previous argument. It suggests what must happen if a pinned distance profile is nearly as small as 34\frac{3}{4}. We now prove that the source must acquire information quickly at the early scales, and that the pin must retain an excess of nearly 14\frac{1}{4} over the trivial profile on an interval of length nearly 14\frac{1}{4}. Both statements are proved at a general transfer level, because a source of dimension larger than one admits a larger level (Section 8.5), and the level enters the final exponent comparison.

8.1 The certificate and the first hitting scale

Throughout this section f,g,dxf,g,d_{x} satisfy the profile bounds (2.3), the prefix estimate (4.2) with xx as the pin, and the transfer estimate for dxd_{x} with H^\widehat{H} (Lemma 7.2). Fix 0≤Δ<120\leq\Delta<\frac{1}{2} and put

λ=1+Δ,F=12+Δ,ac=14+Δ2,W0=1−2​Δ4,q=34+Δ2+ω,\lambda=1+\Delta,\qquad F=\frac{1}{2}+\Delta,\qquad a_{c}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\Delta}{2},\qquad W_{0}=\frac{1-2\Delta}{4},\qquad q=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{\Delta}{2}+\omega, (8.1)

where ω≥0\omega\geq 0. Let a∗a_{*} be the first point with f⁡(a∗)=Ff(a_{*})=F. It exists when f⁡(1)≥Ff(1)\geq F. We say that the pair has the certificate at level λ\lambda if

Hf,g​(a∗,1)≥λ,H_{f,g}(a_{*},1)\geq\lambda, (8.2)

where Hf,gH_{f,g} is the closed transfer functional (4.4). In particular f⁡(1)≥λf(1)\geq\lambda. For Δ=0\Delta=0 the certificate holds for every admissible pair. For a∗≤s≤12a_{*}\leq s\leq\frac{1}{2} one has f⁡(s)≥12f(s)\geq\frac{1}{2} and pg​(s,1)≥12p_{g}(s;1)\geq\frac{1}{2}, for s≥12s\geq\frac{1}{2} one has f⁡(s)≥sf(s)\geq s and pg​(s,1)=1−sp_{g}(s;1)=1-s, and f⁡(1)≥1f(1)\geq 1. Section 8.5 obtains Δ>0\Delta>0 from a source dimension larger than one.

If the pair has the certificate at level λ\lambda and dx​(1)≤qd_{x}(1)\leq q, then

8.2 Partition bounds

For a continuous function hh on a compact interval I=[u,v]I=[u,v] and t>0t>0, define

Lt​(h,I)=inf𝒫∑[a,b]∈𝒫[a,b]​ labelled yellow(h⁡(b)−h⁡(a)),L_{t}(h;I)=\inf_{\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}[a,b]\in\mathcal{P}\\ [a,b]\text{ labelled yellow}\end{subarray}}\bigl(h(b)-h(a)\bigr),

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} ranges over finite yellow–teal partitions of II with piece lengths at most tt, as in Section 7. A yellow piece has its minimum at its left endpoint, and a teal piece has its minimum at its right endpoint. Either label is allowed when both endpoints minimize hh. Set Lt​(h,[u,u])=0L_{t}(h;[u,u])=0. Thus ℒt​(g,R)=Lt​(hg,[0,R])\mathcal{L}_{t}(g;R)=L_{t}(h_{g};[0,R]). The next lemma is the elementary partition bound behind Stull’s projection argument.

Lemma 8.2 (A terminal-minimum partition bound).

Let h:[0,L]→[0,∞)h:[0,L]\to[0,\infty) be 11-Lipschitz, with h⁡(L)=0h(L)=0 and h⁡(0)=ph(0)=p. For every t>0t>0,

Lt​(h,[0,L])≤max⁡{0,L−t−p2}.L_{t}(h;[0,L])\leq\max\{0,\frac{L-t-p}{2}\}. (8.3)

The right side is attained as an upper bound by a partition with at most ⌈2​Lt⌉+8\lceil\frac{2L}{t}\rceil+8 intervals.

Proof.

When L≤tL\leq t the whole interval is teal. First suppose that hh is piecewise linear with slopes 11 and −1-1. Apply the red–green–blue construction preceding [33, Observation 20] to u+h⁡(u)u+h(u). In terms of hh, red means increasing, blue means decreasing, and green means an interval of length at most tt whose two endpoints are equal and minimize hh. This construction uses only the finite polygonal profile. The point-dimension assumption used later in [33, Lemma 21] is not involved here.

If there is a red–green–blue sequence, the construction supplies one or two adjacent green intervals of combined length at least tt. Keep these intervals and partition the two complementary intervals by the ordinary greedy yellow–teal rule. This rule chooses the furthest admissible next endpoint at distance at most tt, labelling the resulting interval teal whenever possible. A non-teal yellow interval has length tt, unless it reaches the terminal endpoint. otherwise continuity permits a further yellow extension. Two successive teal intervals can be merged whenever their combined length is at most tt. Consequently successive greedy endpoints obey ai+2>ai+ta_{i+2}>a_{i}+t, except at the last endpoint, and a subinterval of length ℓ\ell needs at most ⌈2​ℓt⌉+2\lceil\frac{2\ell}{t}\rceil+2 pieces. The partition retaining the green interval or pair therefore has at most ⌈2​Lt⌉+8\lceil\frac{2L}{t}\rceil+8 pieces.

Let UU be its yellow loss and let VV be minus the sum of its teal increments, including the green intervals with increment zero. Then U−V=−pU-V=-p. The 11-Lipschitz bound, and the green length of at least tt, give U+V≤L−tU+V\leq L-t. Thus U≤L−t−p2U\leq\frac{L-t-p}{2}.

If there is no red–green–blue sequence, there can be no red interval in the auxiliary partition. Indeed, after a red interval a later blue interval would give a red–green–blue sequence by choosing the last red preceding the first subsequent blue. The absence of later blue intervals would make the final height strictly greater than a preceding height, since green intervals have zero endpoint increment. This contradicts h⁡(L)=min⁡hh(L)=\min h. The auxiliary partition thus consists only of blue and green intervals. It can be coarsened to an all-teal partition. Greedily choose the furthest teal endpoint at distance at most tt lying outside the interiors of the auxiliary green intervals. Such a next endpoint always exists, because each green interval has length at most tt and the heights at all eligible endpoints are nonincreasing. Two consecutive resulting intervals could be merged if their combined length were at most tt. The same endpoint spacing therefore bounds their number by ⌈2​Lt⌉+2\lceil\frac{2L}{t}\rceil+2. Their loss is zero.

Finally approximate a general hh uniformly by nonnegative finite polygonal functions hjh_{j} with slopes 11 and −1-1, preserving both endpoint values. One construction replaces each linear interpolation segment by a rising-then-falling roof with the same endpoints. The 11-Lipschitz assumption makes that roof possible. Its height above the linear segment is at most the mesh size. The preceding partitions have a uniform cardinality bound. After padding by zero-length intervals, pass to a subsequence on which every endpoint and every colour converges. The endpoint-minimum properties are closed under uniform convergence, as are the length constraints, and the total yellow loss converges. Remove zero-length intervals. The resulting finite partition proves both assertions. ∎

Lemma 8.3 (Endpoint estimates for the partition loss).

Let h:[0,L]→[0,∞)h:[0,L]\to[0,\infty) be 11-Lipschitz with h⁡(0)=p0h(0)=p_{0} and h⁡(L)=p1h(L)=p_{1}. For every t>0t>0,

≤max⁡{p,p+u−t2,p+L−p1−u−t2,L−p1−2​t2}.\displaystyle\leq\max\left\{p,\frac{p+u-t}{2},\frac{p+L-p_{1}-u-t}{2},\frac{L-p_{1}-2t}{2}\right\}.

9   Barriers for the reciprocal estimates

A small distance profile forces both endpoints to carry information before a common cutoff. We first follow that information to later scales. The two barriers proved here will allow us to move the cutoff backwards. The reciprocal argument in the next section retains the separate endpoint values when this common lower bound is no longer enough.

Throughout this section f,g,dx,dyf,g,d_{x},d_{y} satisfy (2.3), the prefix estimate (4.2), the transfer estimate of Lemma 4.1, and the full partition transfer of Lemma 7.2, for both choices of pin, and dx​(1),dy​(1)≤Qd_{x}(1),d_{y}(1)\leq Q. We write hg=g−uh_{g}=g-u as in Section 7, and ℓ=min⁡{f,g}\ell=\min\{f,g\}.

10   Reciprocal estimates at a general transfer level

We now pass the estimates from one endpoint to the other and back again. The level-one conclusion is the scalar bound 45\frac{4}{5}. Keeping the transfer level as a parameter will also account for the source dimension. The essential point is to retain the separate excesses at the early cutoff until they return to the same contact equation at the end of the proof.

In this and the following scalar arguments, a scalar system means four profiles satisfying (2.3), the prefix bounds (4.2), and the closed and full partition transfers of Lemmas 4.1 and 7.2 in both orientations. 12   Matching profiles and the minimum-ratio argument

When the endpoint profiles agree, a single conditioned distance profile satisfies the scalar inequalities in both orientations. We can then choose a scale at which its information per unit precision is nearly smallest. At that scale, every earlier distance prefix has a useful linear lower bound. This additional bound lets the tail iteration reach the full source floor.

14   The source parent and the annular cap

The finite geometry will require a bound on the source mass that can lie both in a small parent square and near one circle. The interval-transfer proof already contains the needed information. Before its last chain rule, the coarse source location is still available as conditioning data. We keep it.

A lower bound for this conditional complexity becomes an upper bound for annular mass by measure coding. The cancellation of the parent mass leaves a bound for every occupied parent and radius bin with respect to the same original source measure.

Corollary 14.3 (Keeping all parents).

An unoccupied cell and radial-bin has zero restricted mass. An occupied one is bounded by the full source mass in (14.2). ∎

At the critical scales, the cap bounds each occupied parent–radius mass by δλ\delta^{\lambda}, up to the stated power loss. Finite selection will retain only source cells carrying a specified fraction of their original mass. Dividing the cap by the least retained cell mass then bounds the number of assigned vertices in each parent on a circle. This is the parent-incidence hypothesis used in Section 17. Figure 4 shows the intersection whose mass is controlled.

Part III Circle graphs, bisectors, and the pinned improvement

15   Perpendicular bisectors and their size

This section separates two notions of size that occur in the proof. Hausdorff dimension measures a fixed family of lines through all small scales. A finite count measures a line family at one specified scale. The proposition below concerns Hausdorff dimension. The finite counts are the subject of Sections 17–19. The identity after the proposition explains how repeated circle incidences produce rich tubes. Both follow directly from elementary geometry.

Proposition 15.1 (Bisectors with one endpoint fixed).

Let y∈ℝ2y\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and F⊂ℝ2∖{y}F\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{y\}. In the line-space metric of Section 2,

dimH{ℬ⁡(y,z):z∈F}=dimHF.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\{\mathcal{B}(y,z):z\in F\}=\dim_{\mathrm{H}}F.

Consequently, if EE has positive Hausdorff dimension and ℬ(E)={ℬ(y,z):y,z∈E,y≠z}\mathcal{B}(E)=\{\mathcal{B}(y,z):y,z\in E,y\neq z\}, then

dimHℬ⁡(E)≥dimHE.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\mathcal{B}(E)\geq\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E.
Proof.

Write z−y=r​nz-y=rn, with r>0r>0 and n∈S1n\in S^{1}. Its bisector has normal nn and offset

c=n⋅y+r2.c=n\cdot y+\frac{r}{2}.

Conversely, reflecting yy across Ln,cL_{n,c} recovers the other endpoint:

z=y+2​(c−n⋅y)​n.z=y+2(c-n\cdot y)n.

The second formula is independent of the choice between (n,c)(n,c) and (−n,−c)(-n,-c). The first map and its inverse are locally Lipschitz away from r=0r=0. Cover the punctured plane by countably many bounded angular charts with rr bounded above and bounded away from zero. On sufficiently small closed subcharts the maps are bi-Lipschitz. Hausdorff dimension is preserved there, and countable stability proves the equality for FF.

For the final assertion fix y∈Ey\in E and apply the equality to F=E∖{y}F=E\setminus\{y\}. Removing one point does not change a positive Hausdorff dimension, and this pinned bisector family is contained in ℬ⁡(E)\mathcal{B}(E). ∎

The approximate bisector relation follows from the identity

|x−y|2−|x−z|2=|y|2−|z|2−2​x⋅(y−z).|x-y|^{2}-|x-z|^{2}=|y|^{2}-|z|^{2}-2x\cdot(y-z).

If the two distances agree to error O⁡(δ)O(\delta) and remain bounded, then xx is within O⁡(δ|y−z|)O(\frac{\delta}{|y-z|}) of ℬ⁡(y,z)\mathcal{B}(y,z). Source separation |y−z|≥c​η|y-z|\geq c\eta makes this a tube of width O⁡(δη)O(\frac{\delta}{\eta}), and separation at a scale δc\delta^{c} with c≤aparc\leq a_{\mathrm{par}} results in the width O⁡(δ1−c)O(\delta^{1-c}) used in Sections 17 and 18. This calculation explains why the circle graph must produce separated pairs rather than just distinct vertices.

16   Drawing approximate circle incidences

In a multigraph, distinct edges may join the same pair of vertices. These are parallel edges, and their number is the multiplicity of the pair. A loop joins a vertex to itself. A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. A complete graph joins every pair of distinct vertices. An independent set of vertices has no edge between any two of its members. These are the graph conventions used below.

Join consecutive assigned source vertices along each circle. This produces a graph with many edges and few crossings, because two distinct circles meet at most twice. The approximate incidences require some care. A circle can enter a source disk without being assigned to its vertex.

Inside each disk we route assigned strands through the vertex and other strands past it. The latter create no new graph incidences. The extra crossings are controlled by the number of circle strands entering the disks. At our cardinalities, this cost is smaller than the main circle-pair count.

A drawing below represents each edge by a simple arc joining its two vertices. Its interior avoids every graph vertex. Overlapping arcs are separated by arbitrarily small perturbations. All interior intersections are transverse, and no three edge interiors meet at one point. A proper intersection is a crossing. Edges may share an endpoint, and that shared endpoint is not counted. The crossing number cr⁡(G)\operatorname{cr}(G) is the least number of crossings over these drawings of GG. We write V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) for its numbers of vertices and edges when a graph argument uses these as numerical quantities.

Lemma 16.1 (Drawing prescribed circle incidences).

Fix R≥1R\geq 1 and 0<d0<D00<d_{0}<D_{0}. Let 0<δ≪d0R0<\delta\ll\frac{d_{0}}{R}, and let VV source vertices pvp_{v} have mutual distances greater than 5​R​δ5R\delta. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a finite set of distinct circles, all with radii in [d0,D0][d_{0},D_{0}], and write C=#​𝒞C=\#\mathcal{C}. Choose pairwise disjoint vertex disks Dv=B⁡(pv,rv)D_{v}=B(p_{v},r_{v}), with R​δ<rv<2​R​δR\delta<r_{v}<2R\delta. Specify an arbitrary set of incidences (v,γ)(v,\gamma) such that γ\gamma meets DvD_{v}. Let II denote their number.

There is a loop-free multigraph GG on the source vertices, with at least I−CI-C edges, obtained by joining consecutive prescribed visits on each circle, and a drawing satisfying

cr⁡(G)≤2​(C2)+4​∑v(kv2),kv=#⁡{γ∈𝒞:γ∩Dv≠∅}.\operatorname{cr}(G)\leq 2\binom{C}{2}+4\sum_{v}\binom{k_{v}}{2},\qquad k_{v}=\#\{\gamma\in\mathcal{C}:\gamma\cap D_{v}\neq\varnothing\}. (16.1)

The disk radii may be chosen generically inside the indicated ranges. No prescribed visit is lost if its circle already meets the smaller disk of radius R​δR\delta.

If the circles are centered at MM distinct pins and, for each pin, their radii are δ\delta-separated, then

cr⁡(G)≤CR​(C2+V​M2).\operatorname{cr}(G)\leq C_{R}(C^{2}+VM^{2}). (16.2)

One may take

CR=2​(⌊4​R⌋+2)2.C_{R}=2(\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2)^{2}.

Every graph edge retains its original circle label and has both endpoints among that circle’s prescribed incidences.

Proof.

Perturb each disk radius sufficiently slightly inside the indicated range, preserving exactly the same circle visits, and avoid the finitely many values that produce a circle tangency to a disk boundary or put a circle–circle intersection on such a boundary. Since rv<d0r_{v}<d_{0}, a circle meeting DvD_{v} has a single proper arc inside it. This follows also directly by writing the disk condition on a circle as one inequality for the cosine of its angular parameter. There is therefore one local strand for each of the kvk_{v} circles.

Inside DvD_{v}, replace an incident strand by the two straight spokes from its boundary points to pvp_{v}. Replace a nonincident strand by a straight chord, or by a generic two-segment polygonal path if a chord would pass through pvp_{v}. All these paths stay in the convex disk. A nonincident path is chosen to avoid pvp_{v}, overlaps, and nonrequired multiple intersections. Each pair of local strands has at most four proper intersections, since each uses at most two straight segments. In particular, incident strands meeting at the common graph vertex do not contribute proper crossings.

Outside the disks retain the original circle arcs. Distinct circles have at most two intersection points, so these portions contribute at most 2​(C2)2\binom{C}{2} crossings. If necessary, an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of the circles, preserving all disk visits, puts their exterior intersections in general position. The same bound holds. Such a perturbation exists because the finite list of boundary incidences was made transverse. The local paths can then be chosen in general position as above.

A circle with k≥2k\geq 2 prescribed visits now contributes kk graph edges between successive prescribed vertices in cyclic order. When k=2k=2 these are two parallel edges, which are allowed. Discard circles with zero or one prescribed visit. The total number of retained edges is at least I−CI-C. A nonprescribed disk passage never creates a graph endpoint. The preceding crossing count proves (16.1).

For a pin xx, a circle of radius rr can meet DvD_{v} only if ||x−pv|−r|≤rv<2​R​δ||x-p_{v}|-r|\leq r_{v}<2R\delta. A δ\delta-separated set of radii has at most ⌊4​R⌋+2\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2 members in this interval. Thus kv≤(⌊4​R⌋+2)​Mk_{v}\leq(\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2)M, proving (16.2) with the stated constant: the two terms in (16.1) are at most C2C^{2} and 2​V​(⌊4​R⌋+2)2​M22V(\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2)^{2}M^{2}. ∎

The angular span of a row about a pin xx is the smallest interval in its chosen angular chart containing the angles arg⁡(v−x)\arg(v-x) of its entries vv. Its length is the angular diameter. An angular window is an interval in that chart.

Corollary 16.2 (Clique edges in disjoint circle rows).

Assume the hypotheses of Lemma 16.1, including that the circles are centered at MM distinct pins and have δ\delta-separated radii at each pin. On each circle choose disjoint rows of at most ss prescribed source vertices, in circular order, such that their angular spans have disjoint interiors. Draw all edges of the complete graph on each row, retaining parallel edges from different rows or circles. For each fixed ss this multigraph has a drawing satisfying

cr⁡(Gs)≤CR,s​(C2+V​M2).\operatorname{cr}(G_{s})\leq C_{R,s}(C^{2}+VM^{2}). (16.3)

For example, the construction below permits

CR,s=32​(s2)2​(⌊4​R⌋+2)2.C_{R,s}=32\binom{s}{2}^{2}(\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2)^{2}.

No incidence with an unselected vertex is added.

Proof.

Within a row, label an edge by the ordered pair (i,j)(i,j) of the positions of its endpoints. For each circle there are at most L=(s2)L=\binom{s}{2} such labels. For a fixed label, the supporting arcs in different row spans have disjoint interiors.

Use LL arbitrarily close concentric circle tracks for each original circle, one per label. The tracks can be chosen to preserve all disk visits, as in the proof of Lemma 16.1. Support each selected edge on its track between its two endpoint disks. It may pass other disks without being incident to their vertices. Distinct tracks are circles, hence have at most two exterior intersections, and at most one selected edge occupies any given track arc. Their total exterior crossing count is therefore Os​(C2)O_{s}(C^{2}).

Fix one disk visit of one track. Its exterior support is a union of arcs with disjoint interiors: the edge label is fixed and the row spans on this circle have disjoint interiors. At each of the two boundary points of the visit, at most one supported edge arc can enter the disk. Thus the visit carries at most two incident ends, or one passage, or a combination bounded by these two boundary ports. Route each incident end to pvp_{v} by a spoke, and each passage by a chord or a generic two-segment path avoiding pvp_{v}. Figure 6 illustrates these rules. With LL tracks for each of the kvk_{v} original circle visits, there are at most 2​L​kv2Lk_{v} local paths. The more generous bound 4​L​kv4Lk_{v} permits endpoint splitting and generic perturbations. The same two-segment construction produces at most

4​(4​L​kv2)=2​(4​L​kv)​(4​L​kv−1)≤32​L2​kv24\binom{4Lk_{v}}{2}=2(4Lk_{v})(4Lk_{v}-1)\leq 32L^{2}k_{v}^{2}

local crossings. The exterior crossing count is at most 2​(L​C2)≤L2​C22\binom{LC}{2}\leq L^{2}C^{2}. Since kv≤(⌊4​R⌋+2)​Mk_{v}\leq(\lfloor 4R\rfloor+2)M, summation proves (16.3) with the displayed choice of CR,sC_{R,s}. All local replacements stay inside their respective disks. If a replacement creates a self-intersection of an edge, erase the loop. This removes intersections and adds no vertex. A final arbitrarily small perturbation produces simple edge arcs in general position without increasing the displayed bound. All graph endpoints were prescribed row vertices throughout. ∎

Lemma 16.3 (Parallel edges give approximate bisector richness).

In the first lemma, if vertices p≠qp\neq q have graph multiplicity mG​(p,q)m_{G}(p,q), the number of edges joining them, then at least cR​mG​(p,q)c_{R}m_{G}(p,q) distinct pins lie within distance

CR,D0​δ|p−q|C_{R,D_{0}}\frac{\delta}{|p-q|}

of the perpendicular bisector of p,qp,q. For the row-clique graph the same statement holds with constants also depending on ss.

Proof.

A circle contributes at most two edges to a fixed pair in the cyclic graph. Each pin has at most CRC_{R} circle radii meeting the disk of pp, so at least cR​mG​(p,q)c_{R}m_{G}(p,q) distinct pins support the parallel edges. The row-clique graph has a similarly bounded number of contributions per circle and pair, with a constant depending only on ss.

If a circle centered at xx meets both disks, then

||x−p|−|x−q||≤rp+rq≤4​R​δ.\big||x-p|-|x-q|\big|\leq r_{p}+r_{q}\leq 4R\delta.

The expression on the left equals twice |p−q||p-q| times the distance of xx from the bisector. This proves the claim. The labels in the drawing refer to the original circles, so auxiliary track perturbations introduce no change in this distance calculation. ∎

Lemma 16.4 (Localized drawing).

In the setting of Corollary 16.2, suppose in addition that every row has angular diameter at most C​wCw about its pin, where δ≪w≪1\delta\ll w\ll 1, and that each source vertex belongs to at most CC rows at any one pin. For a square QQ of a grid of mesh ww, let VQV_{Q} be the number of source vertices in a fixed enlargement of QQ. Then the drawing can be chosen with

cr⁡(Gs)≤CR,s​M2​(∑QVQ2+V)≤CR,s​M2​V​(1+maxQ⁡VQ).\operatorname{cr}(G_{s})\leq C_{R,s}M^{2}\Bigl(\sum_{Q}V_{Q}^{2}+V\Bigr)\leq C_{R,s}M^{2}V\Bigl(1+\max_{Q}V_{Q}\Bigr). (16.4)

Use the drawing of Corollary 16.2. Every exterior edge is the short track arc between its endpoint disks inside its row span. Distinct tracks meet at most twice and arcs of different rows on one track have disjoint interiors, so the crossings charged to QQ number at most C​(M​VQ)2C(MV_{Q})^{2}. For source representatives in distinct terminal δ\delta-squares, the required disk separation can be arranged by a fixed finite coloring of the grid. A color retaining a fixed fraction of the prescribed incidences is sufficient. In the configuration of Section 17, V≲pbV\lesssim\frac{p}{b}, M≲υf−1M\lesssim\upsilon_{f}^{-1}, and C≲υf−1​δ−qC\lesssim\upsilon_{f}^{-1}\delta^{-q}, so the two terms in (16.3) are O⁡(υf−2​δ−2​q)O(\upsilon_{f}^{-2}\delta^{-2q}) and O⁡(p​υf−2​b−1)O(p\upsilon_{f}^{-2}b^{-1}). The second is the smaller one because p​δ2​q≤bp\delta^{2q}\leq b. Thus local detours do not introduce a new loss.

17   Circle graphs produce rows with rich bisectors

The reason for drawing the graph can be seen from the counts. After a thinning of the source described below, the source vertices number about pb\frac{p}{b}, the circles about υf−1​δ−q\upsilon_{f}^{-1}\delta^{-q}, and the rows about p2n​b​υf\frac{p^{2}}{nb\upsilon_{f}}, where the symbols are introduced next. A simple graph with these many vertices and edges would have more crossings than the drawing of Section 16 allows. Hence many edges must be repeated.

For a source pair, repetition means that many circles from different pins visit both endpoints. Those pins lie near the perpendicular bisector. We need this conclusion for every pair in a row of fixed length, so we draw all pairs within each row and discard rows containing a pair of low multiplicity. Two further steps sharpen the conclusion. An ordered selection inside each row extracts shorter rows whose pair separations lie between two consecutive scales. The drawing of these rows can then be localized, which increases the multiplicity of their pairs. Finally the pins are thinned to the resolution of the resulting bisector tubes.

17.2 One thinning of the source for all pins

A thinning retains each point independently with a specified probability. We write ℙ\mathbb{P} for probability, 𝔼​Z\mathbb{E}Z for expectation, and Var⁡(Z)=𝔼​(Z−𝔼​Z)2\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\mathbb{E}(Z-\mathbb{E}Z)^{2} for variance. We use Markov’s inequality ℙ{Z≥t}≤𝔼​Zt\mathbb{P}\{Z\geq t\}\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}Z}{t} for Z≥0Z\geq 0, and Chebyshev’s inequality ℙ{|Z−𝔼Z|≥t}≤Var⁡(Z)t2\mathbb{P}\{|Z-\mathbb{E}Z|\geq t\}\leq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{t^{2}}. For a sum ZZ of independent zero-one variables with mean mm, the Chernoff bounds used below are

ℙ{Z<12m}≤e−m8,ℙ{Z≥m+t}≤exp(−t22​(m+t3))for t>0.\mathbb{P}\{Z<\frac{1}{2}m\}\leq\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{m}{8}},\qquad\mathbb{P}\{Z\geq m+t\}\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2(m+\frac{t}{3})}\right)\quad\text{for }t>0.

See [1, Chapters 2, 4 and Appendix A]. The union bound adds the failure probabilities over all events. With at most 2C​n2^{Cn} events, the upper-tail estimate ensures Z≤C′​(m+n)Z\leq C^{\prime}(m+n) for all of them with probability tending to one, by taking C′C^{\prime} sufficiently large. These are the simultaneous sampling bounds used in this and the subsequent sections.

The simultaneous requirement is essential. A related probabilistic selection appears in Shmerkin–Yavicoli [32, Lemmas 3.4 and 3.6], where one small set must work for a whole family of sumsets. Their discrete argument is adapted from Ruzsa, as explained there. Here the selected vertices must preserve both the total incidence count and the upper occupancy bounds at every retained pin. The following proof establishes these properties for one source sample.

Lemma 17.1 (One simultaneous source restriction).

For every sufficiently large nn, there is a subset S′⊂SS^{\prime}\subset S such that, retaining the marked incidences with vertices in S′S^{\prime}, the following hold.

#​S′\displaystyle\#S^{\prime} ≤C​pb,\displaystyle\leq\frac{Cp}{b}, I′\displaystyle I^{\prime} ≥c​p2b​υf,\displaystyle\geq\frac{cp^{2}}{b\upsilon_{f}}, (17.5)

A square QQ of side ≍δa\asymp\delta^{a} meets O⁡((δaη)2)O((\frac{\delta^{a}}{\eta})^{2}) squares of side η\eta, each of mass at most δF−τ0\delta^{F-\tau_{0}} if it contains a vertex of SS, and in branch 1 with a≥ac−ωa\geq a_{c}-\omega it is covered by O⁡(1)O(1) dyadic squares of side ≍δa\asymp\delta^{a}, each of mass at most δa+ac−(1+u0+𝔢)​ω−τ0\delta^{a+a_{c}-(1+u_{0}+\mathfrak{e})\omega-\tau_{0}} if it contains a vertex of SS, both by (F3). 17.3 Rows with rich bisectors

The degree of a pin in a collection of rows means the number of rows assigned to it. To regularize degrees dyadically, divide positive degrees into intervals [2j,2j+1)[2^{j},2^{j+1}) and retain one class. When there are O⁡(n)O(n) classes, one carries at least an O​(n)−1O(n)^{-1} fraction of the total count being divided.

Independently for each bundle of k≤k1k\leq k_{1} parallel edges, retain the bundle with probability kk1\frac{k}{k_{1}} and then choose one of its edges uniformly. The resulting random graph is simple, with expected edge count Ek1\frac{E}{k_{1}} and expected crossing count at most Xk12\frac{X}{k_{1}^{2}}: each edge survives with probability 1k1\frac{1}{k_{1}}, edges from distinct bundles are independent, and two edges of one bundle cannot both survive. A witness of a source pair is a pin supporting an assigned occurrence of both vertices on one circle. The width of this tube depends on the separation of the pair. The next step selects rows whose pair separations all lie between two consecutive candidate scales.

18   Counting the bisector directions

The circle argument produces, at each pin of P′P^{\prime}, rows in which every pair has a rich bisector. We now choose one pair from every row so that the chosen directions are spread at every scale between ρ\rho and one. The restricted-sum estimate controls the number of distinct directions that any set of rows can produce, and a max-flow argument turns this into a simultaneous choice. The Furstenberg estimate of Ren and Wang then provides a lower bound for the number of distinct tubes. All results in this section are finite and make no information-theoretic assumptions.

18.1 The restricted-sum estimate

For an n×sn\times s real matrix A=(ai​j)A=(a_{ij}) let S(A)={ai​j+ai​k:i,j,k∈ℕ, 1≤i≤n,1≤j<k≤s}S(A)=\{a_{ij}+a_{ik}:i,j,k\in\mathbb{N},\ 1\leq i\leq n,1\leq j<k\leq s\} be the set of pairwise sums of entries from a common row, and let fs​(n)f_{s}(n) be the minimum of |S⁡(A)||S(A)| over all such matrices whose s​nsn entries are pairwise distinct. The direction of the bisector of a pair is determined, up to O⁡(ρ)O(\rho) and a fixed rotation, by the half-sum of the two source angles. This description also explains the connection with the near-additive-energy estimate of [24, Lemma 19], which counts pairs of sums that differ by at most a prescribed error. Such an estimate for the angular rows could control clustering of their directions. The lacunarity used in that lemma is unavailable here. Moreover, the selection below requires bounds for every subfamily of rows and at each relevant scale. A replacement would have to provide that uniform control while retaining the number of rows needed by the incidence argument.

A flow on a directed network assigns a nonnegative amount to each arc, no larger than its capacity, and conserves total inflow and outflow except at the source and sink. Its value is the net flow out of the source. A cut separates the source from the sink. Its capacity is the sum of capacities of arcs leaving the source side. The original max-flow min-cut theorem appears in [9]. For the directed networks with integer capacities used here, start with zero flow. Each arc has a forward residual arc of capacity equal to its unused capacity and a reverse residual arc of capacity equal to its flow. Retain only arcs of positive residual capacity. Augment along a residual source–sink path by its minimum residual capacity, increasing flow on forward arcs and decreasing it on reverse arcs. Flows remain integral, and every augmentation increases the value by at least one. The value is bounded by the total capacity leaving the source, so the process terminates. When no residual path remains, the vertices reachable from the source determine a cut whose outgoing arcs are saturated and whose incoming arcs carry zero flow. The flow value equals this cut capacity, and every flow value is at most any cut capacity. This proves maximality and integrality.

Build a network with a source joined to every row by an arc of capacity one, every row joined to each of its output leaves by an arc of capacity RR, every tree interval II joined to its parent by an arc of capacity ⌈c⁡(I)⌉\lceil c(I)\rceil, and the root joined to the sink by an arc of capacity RR. Every cut of capacity less than RR leaves some rows UU joined to the source and must separate all their leaves from the root by tree arcs. The highest such arcs on the leaf–root paths form a covering antichain, so the cut has capacity at least R−#​U+∑𝒜⌈c⁡(I)⌉≥RR-\#U+\sum_{\mathcal{A}}\lceil c(I)\rceil\geq R. By the integral-flow argument above there is an integral flow of value RR, that is, one output per row, with at most ⌈c⁡(I)⌉\lceil c(I)\rceil chosen outputs in each tree interval II. Since w≳ρ≫bw\gtrsim\rho\gg b, every c⁡(I)c(I) is at least a fixed constant, so the ceilings change only constants, and an arbitrary interval is covered by O⁡(1)O(1) tree intervals of comparable length. Dividing by 𝔡′≳polb−1\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}\gtrsim_{\mathrm{pol}}b^{-1} proves the second line of (18.1), after accounting for the bounded overlap of the windows. For |J|≥w|J|\geq w, every row with chosen output in JJ has its entries in a fixed enlargement of JJ, so there are O⁡(|J|b)O(\frac{|J|}{b}) such rows, which proves the first line.

To obtain the stated exponent, for ρ≤|J|≤w\rho\leq|J|\leq w write |J|=δu|J|=\delta^{u} with a≤u≤ζa\leq u\leq\zeta. Then α​u+(1−α)​a−sact​u=(1−α)​a​(1−uζ)≥0\alpha u+(1-\alpha)a-s_{\mathrm{act}}u=(1-\alpha)a(1-\frac{u}{\zeta})\geq 0, so |J|α​w1−α≤|J|sact|J|^{\alpha}w^{1-\alpha}\leq|J|^{s_{\mathrm{act}}}. For |J|≥w|J|\geq w, |J|≤|J|sact|J|\leq|J|^{s_{\mathrm{act}}}. ∎

18.3 The Furstenberg estimate and the tube family

We use the discretized Furstenberg estimate of Ren and Wang. For a dyadic square QQ of side ρ\rho in slope–intercept parameter space, the corresponding dyadic ρ\rho-tube is

⋃(a,b)∈Q{(u,v)∈ℝ2:v=a​u+b},\bigcup_{(a,b)\in Q}\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:v=au+b\},

restricted to the fixed bounded spatial region under consideration. Its central line has the parameters of the midpoint of QQ. We work in bounded-slope charts. In the Ren–Wang chart the slopes lie in [−1,1][-1,1]. These tubes have width comparable to ρ\rho on the bounded regions used here [28, Definition 2.3]. For dyadic ρ\rho, a finite family ℱ\mathcal{F} of dyadic ρ\rho-squares or dyadic ρ\rho-tubes is a (ρ,s,C)(\rho,s,C)-set if #⁡{members of ​ℱ​ meeting ​B}≤C​rs​#​ℱ\#\{\text{members of }\mathcal{F}\text{ meeting }B\}\leq Cr^{s}\#\mathcal{F} for every ball BB of radius r∈[ρ,1]r\in[\rho,1] in the respective parameter space [28, Definitions 1.3 and 2.3]. For tubes, this count is taken over their defining squares in slope–intercept parameter space. A pair (𝒫,𝒯)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T}) is a (ρ,s,C,M)(\rho,s,C,M)-nice configuration if every p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} is assigned a (ρ,s,C)(\rho,s,C)-set 𝒯⁡(p)⊂𝒯\mathcal{T}(p)\subset\mathcal{T} with #​𝒯​(p)∼M\#\mathcal{T}(p)\sim M and T∩p≠∅T\cap p\neq\varnothing for all T∈𝒯⁡(p)T\in\mathcal{T}(p) [28, Definition 3.1].

Theorem 18.3 (Ren–Wang, [28, Theorem 4.1]).

Let s∈(0,1]s\in(0,1], t∈(0,2]t\in(0,2], and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. #𝒯≳ϵρ−min⁡{t,s+t2,1}+ϵM.\#\mathcal{T}\gtrsim_{\epsilon}\rho^{-\min\{t,\frac{s+t}{2},1\}+\epsilon}M.

19   Rectangular sampling and rich incidences

The upper bound for the rich tubes comes from an incidence theorem of Fu, Gan and Ren for balls that are spread on a rectangular grid. In this section a tube is a fixed-length neighborhood of width C​ρC\rho of a line in a bounded region, and separation refers to the line parameters of Section 2 in a fixed finite collection of charts. For ρ>0\rho>0, a family of ρ\rho-balls, or of ρ\rho-tubes, is essentially distinct if the intersection of two members has at most half the area of either member. Tk​(ℬ)T_{k}(\mathcal{B}) denotes the set of essentially distinct ρ\rho-tubes meeting more than kk balls of ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Theorem 19.1 (Fu–Gan–Ren, [10, Theorem 3]).

Let 1≤U≤V≤ρ−11\leq U\leq V\leq\rho^{-1}, and divide [0,1]2[0,1]^{2} into U−1×V−1U^{-1}\times V^{-1} rectangles. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a family of ρ\rho-balls with at most one ball in each rectangle. For every σ>0\sigma>0 and every k>max⁡{ρ1−2​σ​U​V,1}k>\max\{\rho^{1-2\sigma}UV,1\},

#Tk(ℬ)≲σρ−σ#ℬUVk−2(k−1+U−1).\#T_{k}(\mathcal{B})\lesssim_{\sigma}\rho^{-\sigma}\#\mathcal{B}UVk^{-2}\bigl(k^{-1}+U^{-1}\bigr). (19.1)

A parameter-separated family splits into a bounded number of essentially distinct families, since overlap exceeding half the area forces parameter distance O⁡(ρ)O(\rho), and separation bounds the degree of this conflict graph. The same holds for balls about a separated set. These bounded colorings, fixed dilations, and fixed similarities affect only constants, and allow (19.1) to be used for the separated pins and tubes of the circle construction.

Lemma 19.2 (Rectangular sampling).

Let XX be a ρ\rho-separated set of NN points in a fixed bounded region. Suppose ρ≤c0​h≤c0​R≤c0\rho\leq c_{0}h\leq c_{0}R\leq c_{0}, with c0>0c_{0}>0 sufficiently small, and

20   From measures to finite configurations

We now return to the measures and construct the finite sets needed by the incidence theorem. The main requirement is that all pins see vertices from one common source set. Separate discretizations for separate pins would not give a graph on which the crossing argument could be used.

We keep the original measures and the original oracle throughout. The pins are actual points, with their full oracles available. Source vertices are centers of small dyadic squares, so their incidences with circles have error O⁡(δ)O(\delta). An assigned incidence records a relation retained by the selection. A circle merely passing close to a source vertex need not be assigned to it.

Lemma 20.4 (Classical bad pins give one recurrent product relation).

Let K⊂ℝ2K\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be compact with dimHK>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}K>1, and let q>0q>0. If

The angular-density and fixed-threshold restrictions used above can be imposed on GG while preserving positive measure. For the resulting relations RnR_{n} and masses PnP_{n}, one has ∑nPn=∞\sum_{n}P_{n}=\infty and Pn≥n−2P_{n}\geq n^{-2} for infinitely many nn. Every limiting source profile of a pair of GG satisfies f⁡(u)≥(1+κ)​uf(u)\geq(1+\kappa)u, every pin xx of a pair of GG satisfies dimAx≥1+ϰ\dim^{A}x\geq 1+\varkappa, and ν⁡(B⁡(z,r))≤C​r1+ϰ\nu(B(z,r))\leq Cr^{1+\varkappa} for every ball.

Proof.

The map x↦Δx​Kx\mapsto\Delta_{x}K is continuous into the space of compact sets with the Hausdorff metric. The condition that a compact set has dimension less than qq is Borel. Express it using a rational exponent below qq and, for every integer mm, the existence of a finite rational open cover with diameters and total exponent cost less than 1m\frac{1}{m}. Thus BqB_{q} is Borel. Frostman’s lemma and compact extraction give probability measures with the prescribed exponents on compact subsets of KK and of BqB_{q}. By restricting to two disjoint small balls carrying positive mass, and then to compact positive-mass subsets, arrange separated supports. The exponents are unchanged. Denote the compact source support by K′⊂KK^{\prime}\subset K.

Use the encoding described in Section 5 to choose one oracle AA making the fixed compact supports effectively compact and both measures computable, including their dyadic masses. The same oracle is used for every pin and every precision. Lemma 2.2, first with B=(A,x)B=(A,x) and then with the endpoints exchanged, establishes both full-oracle independence estimates on a product-full Borel relation, by Fubini. It also proves the base-oracle dyadic mass identities. The Frostman bounds give both effective dimensions greater than one. More precisely, the source coding identity and μ⁡(Qk​(y))≤C​2−(1+κ)​k\mu(Q_{k}(y))\leq C2^{-(1+\kappa)k} give KkA​(y)≥(1+κ)​k−Oy​(log⁡(k+2))K_{k}^{A}(y)\geq(1+\kappa)k-O_{y}(\log(k+2)), so every limiting source profile satisfies f⁡(u)≥(1+κ)​uf(u)\geq(1+\kappa)u. The same argument with ν\nu gives KkA​(x)≥(1+ϰ)​k−Ox​(log⁡(k+2))K_{k}^{A}(x)\geq(1+\varkappa)k-O_{x}(\log(k+2)), hence dimAx≥1+ϰ\dim^{A}x\geq 1+\varkappa, for ν\nu-almost every pin. Include this condition in the product-full relation. Radial absolute continuity and the arclength-null angular complexity deficiency sets give the directional hypotheses for both choices of pin, as in Proposition 5.1. This establishes the fixed-pair hypotheses for arbitrary computable Frostman measures, not only for normalized Hausdorff restrictions. For each pin in the chosen support, Δx​K′\Delta_{x}K^{\prime} is effectively compact relative to (A,x)(A,x). The restricted point-to-set principle therefore implies, for every y∈K′y\in K^{\prime},

dimA,x|x−y|≤dimHΔx​K′≤dimHΔx​K<q.\dim^{A,x}|x-y|\leq\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}K^{\prime}\leq\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}K<q.

Consequently every such pair has infinitely many scales with KnA,x​(|x−y|)≤q​nK_{n}^{A,x}(|x-y|)\leq qn. This uses one common oracle AA. No family of separately chosen pin-dependent point-to-set oracles is being encoded.

Intersect the full-measure good-pair relation with the bounded radial density restriction and then the fixed-threshold restrictions described above. The resulting fixed relation GG has positive pair measure, and every pair still has infinitely many low-distance scales. Tonelli’s theorem implies ∑nPn=∫G∑n1Rn​d​(ν×μ)=∞\sum_{n}P_{n}=\int_{G}\sum_{n}1_{R_{n}}d(\nu\times\mu)=\infty. Since ∑nn−2<∞\sum_{n}n^{-2}<\infty, infinitely many PnP_{n} are at least n−2n^{-2}. ∎

We have obtained a common finite source set, separated actual pins, and assigned circle incidences with the required angular and parent bounds. The preceding circle and bisector estimates now apply to this configuration. We complete the parameter calculation in the next section.

21   The universal pinned improvement

All parts of the pinned argument are now available. We first record the exponents of the configuration produced by Corollary 20.3 and the selections of Sections 17 and 18, then show that they are incompatible with the two tube counts. The parameters are chosen before the set and its measures. The measures determine how far out in the precision sequence we must go, but do not change the threshold.

All these choices precede the set and its measures.

Let KK be compact with dimHK>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}K>1, and suppose that its bad-pin set at threshold qq has dimension greater than one. Lemma 20.4 supplies separated Frostman measures μ,ν\mu,\nu with exponents greater than one, one oracle AA, and one positive-measure relation GG whose low-distance relations have masses Pn≥n−2P_{n}\geq n^{-2} at arbitrarily large precisions. Every pair of GG has the certificate at level 11 (Section 8). Corollary 20.3 supplies, at each such precision, a template, mass classes with p≥c​n−𝔫−4p\geq cn^{-\mathfrak{n}-4}, and the finite inputs (F1)–(F4). The scale conditions of Section 17 hold: ρminb​n→∞\frac{\rho_{\min}}{bn}\to\infty and δ2​qb→0\frac{\delta^{2q}}{b}\to 0 by (17.4), and (17.12) follows from (21.8). Propositions 17.3, 17.5, and 17.6, Lemma 17.7, Lemma 18.2, and Proposition 18.4 produce the pins PP and the tubes 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and Proposition 21.1 excludes the configuration for all sufficiently small δ\delta. Since the recurrent precisions are unbounded, this is a contradiction, and the bad-pin set of KK has dimension at most one. All finite choices are made after the oracle is fixed. They need not be computable or consistent at different precisions.

For analytic EE with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1, choose a compact K⊂EK\subset E of dimension greater than one. Since Δx​K⊂Δx​E\Delta_{x}K\subset\Delta_{x}E for every pin, the bad-pin set of EE at threshold qq is contained in that of KK. The bad-pin set of EE at threshold q∗q_{*} is the countable union over jj of its bad-pin sets at the thresholds 34+ωj\frac{3}{4}+\omega_{j}, the jjth treated with α=αj\alpha=\alpha_{j}. Remark 21.2 (Dependence of the threshold on the measures).

The constants suppressed in ≲pol\lesssim_{\mathrm{pol}}, the angular density bound LL, the uniformization thresholds of Lemma 20.2, and the coding constants of Lemma 20.4 depend on the fixed measures μ,ν\mu,\nu and on the relation GG: through the Frostman constants and support diameters, the source–pin separation, and the fixed constants of the drawing lemmas. The proof uses only that they are independent of the precision nn. They are not bounded in terms of the Frostman exponents or of dimHE\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E alone: the uniformization thresholds come from Borel–Cantelli arguments without a rate, and LL is chosen so that a restriction retains positive mass. Consequently the scale below which the finite configuration is excluded depends on the measures, whereas the incidence parameters and the threshold are fixed before the set and the measures are chosen. The source dimension enters only through the level of the certificate. The theorem is a dimension bound, for which the existence of arbitrarily large admissible scales is all that is needed. No effective threshold in terms of the dimension is claimed. This dependence already enters the information-to-measure step, through the almost-sure coding lemma, before the finite geometric argument is applied.

22   Two-sided angular bounds and bisector witnesses

We retain the notation of Sections 17 and 18. The source and pin sets are related by assigned incidences. Previously we controlled the directions of the source vertices from each pin. We now also control the directions of the assigned pins from each source vertex. Near a perpendicular bisector, this second angular estimate becomes a bound for the number of witnesses in a small square.

All source and pin locations are in fixed bounded sets at positive distance from each other. Constants may depend on this separation, on the diameter bounds, and on the fixed incidence error. Directions are in S1S^{1}. Using finitely many angular charts changes constants only.

Let PP be a pin set and let I⊂P×VI\subset P\times V be the assigned incidence relation with a common finite source set VV. Assume, for each v∈Vv\in V and every angular interval JJ of length at least ρ\rho, that

#{x∈P:(x,v)∈I,arg(x−v)∈J}≤C0N0(|J|+ρ).\#\{x\in P:(x,v)\in I,\arg(x-v)\in J\}\leq C_{0}N_{0}(|J|+\rho). (22.1)

Here N0N_{0} is a cardinality normalization, comparable to #​P\#P up to the allowed polynomial factors. The rest of this section explains how to supply (22.1) in the construction of Section 20.

For distinct v,z∈Vv,z\in V put ℓ=|v−z|\ell=|v-z| and ρℓ=δℓ\rho_{\ell}=\frac{\delta}{\ell}. Let 𝒲⁡(v,z)\mathcal{W}(v,z) consist of assigned common-incidence witnesses satisfying

(x,v),(x,z)∈I,||x−v|−|x−z||≤C​δ.(x,v),(x,z)\in I,\qquad\bigl||x-v|-|x-z|\bigr|\leq C\delta.

Any subcollection, in particular the witnesses from actual row occurrences, may be used. It is essential to keep this assigned-incidence condition. Whenever the grid 𝒟D\mathcal{D}_{D} is used in the following count, DD is a dyadic side length.

Theorem 22.1.

Suppose (22.1) holds with ρ≤C​ρℓ\rho\leq C\rho_{\ell}, and ρℓ≤c​ℓ\rho_{\ell}\leq c\ell. For every square QQ of side D≥ρℓD\geq\rho_{\ell},

#⁡(𝒲⁡(v,z)∩Q)≤C​C0​N0​(ℓ​D+ρℓ).\#(\mathcal{W}(v,z)\cap Q)\leq CC_{0}N_{0}(\ell D+\rho_{\ell}). (22.2)

Consequently, if #​𝒲​(v,z)≥k\#\mathcal{W}(v,z)\geq k, then

#⁡{Q∈𝒟D:Q∩𝒲⁡(v,z)≠∅}≥kC​C0​N0​(ℓ​D+ρℓ).\#\{Q\in\mathcal{D}_{D}:Q\cap\mathcal{W}(v,z)\neq\varnothing\}\geq\frac{k}{CC_{0}N_{0}(\ell D+\rho_{\ell})}. (22.3)

Without the comparison ρ≤C​ρℓ\rho\leq C\rho_{\ell}, the same conclusions hold with ℓ​D+ρℓ+ρ\ell D+\rho_{\ell}+\rho in place of ℓ​D+ρℓ\ell D+\rho_{\ell}.

Proof.

The squared-distance identity places the witnesses in the C​ρℓC\rho_{\ell}-neighborhood of the perpendicular bisector LL of v,zv,z. The distance from vv to LL is ℓ2\frac{\ell}{2}. A segment of LL of length O⁡(D)O(D), at distance bounded above and below from vv, has radial image as viewed from vv of angular length O⁡(ℓ​D)O(\ell D): the derivative of its angle with respect to arclength is

dist⁡(v,L)|x−v|2=O⁡(ℓ).\frac{\operatorname{dist}(v,L)}{|x-v|^{2}}=O(\ell).

Thickening the segment by O⁡(ρℓ)O(\rho_{\ell}) enlarges its radial image by O⁡(ρℓ)O(\rho_{\ell}). Intersecting with the pin region, and splitting into a bounded number of segments if necessary, shows that the radial image of Q∩L(C​ρℓ)Q\cap L^{(C\rho_{\ell})} is covered by boundedly many arcs of total length O⁡(ℓ​D+ρℓ)O(\ell D+\rho_{\ell}). Apply (22.1) to these arcs, enlarging short arcs to the resolution ρ\rho. This proves (22.2). Summing over occupied DD-squares proves (22.3). ∎

22.1 Preserving both angular bounds

The additional condition is available from the common relation, but it requires changing the deterministic choice of finite pin representatives.

Lemma 22.2 (Two-sided angular restriction).

Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be separated compactly supported planar Frostman probability measures, both of exponent strictly greater than one. Any Borel relation GG of positive ν×μ\nu\times\mu measure has a positive-measure restriction G′G^{\prime} and a finite LL such that

(πx)∗​(μ|Gx′)≤L​ℋ1,(πy)∗​(ν|(G′)y)≤L​ℋ1(\pi_{x})_{*}(\mu|_{G^{\prime}_{x}})\leq L\mathcal{H}^{1},\qquad(\pi_{y})_{*}(\nu|_{(G^{\prime})^{y}})\leq L\mathcal{H}^{1}

for almost every relevant x,yx,y, respectively.

Proof.

Orponen’s radial absolute continuity theorem [25], applied in both orientations, establishes absolute continuity for almost every center with respect to the other measure: the exceptional dimension is strictly less than one, so the other Frostman measure assigns it mass zero. Choose measurable versions of the two radial densities. Restrict GG to pairs where both densities evaluated at the pair’s direction are at most LL. These restrictions increase, as L→∞L\to\infty, to a product-full subset of GG. Choose finite LL retaining positive mass. Each restricted fiber has angular pushforward bounded by its truncated original density. ∎

The restriction is fixed before the recurrent low-distance precisions are selected. Every subsequent subrelation inherits these bounds.

Lemma 22.3 (Random representatives retain both angular bounds).

Use Lemma 20.1, with source δ\delta-cell masses in [m,2​m)[m,2m), fine pin-cell masses in [v,2​v)[v,2v), and relation mass p≥n−Cp\geq n^{-C}, where δ=2−n\delta=2^{-n}. If the relation has both angular bounds of Lemma 22.2, its finite representatives can be chosen so that all original forward estimates hold and, simultaneously for every source-cell center vQv_{Q},

#{x∈ℝ2:(x,vQ) is assigned,arg(x−vQ)∈J}≲polv−1(|J|+δ)+O(n)\#\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:(x,v_{Q})\text{ is assigned},\arg(x-v_{Q})\in J\}\lesssim_{\mathrm{pol}}v^{-1}(|J|+\delta)+O(n) (22.4)

at every dyadic angular scale. Polynomial factors depend on n,p−1n,p^{-1} and the fixed measure constants.

Proof.

First perform the active cell and radial-bin selection in the proof of Lemma 20.1. An assigned source cell QQ has active fiber mass at least τ​μ​(Q)\tau\mu(Q), with τ≳pol1\tau\gtrsim_{\mathrm{pol}}1, and the surviving active relation has mass ≳polp\gtrsim_{\mathrm{pol}}p. Choose one independent point xBx_{B} from each relevant fine pin cell BB, with law ν|Bν⁡(B)\frac{\nu|_{B}}{\nu(B)}, and discard samples with no active assignments.

For a source cell QQ and an angular interval JJ, the indicator that xx assigns QQ and arg⁡(x−vQ)∈J\arg(x-v_{Q})\in J is bounded by

1τ​μ​(Q)∫Q1G′(x,y)1{arg(x−y)∈J(C​δ)}dμ(y).\frac{1}{\tau\mu(Q)}\int_{Q}1_{G^{\prime}}(x,y)1_{\{\arg(x-y)\in J^{(C\delta)}\}}d\mu(y).

This uses the active-mass lower bound and the fixed source–pin separation. Integrate in xx over the pin cells and use ν⁡(B)≥v\nu(B)\geq v. Fubini and the reverse angular bound give the expectation at most

C​L​(|J|+δ)τ​v.\frac{CL(|J|+\delta)}{\tau v}.

The count is a sum of independent indicators. A Chernoff upper tail, with an additive sufficiently large multiple of nn, holds simultaneously for every source cell and every dyadic angular interval: there are only polynomially many in δ−1\delta^{-1}. Arbitrary intervals follow by a bounded dyadic cover at comparable scale.

The original incidence lower bound also survives this random choice. If F⁡(x)F(x) counts active assignments, then F⁡(x)≲m−1F(x)\lesssim m^{-1}, while the expected total is ≳polpm​v\gtrsim_{\mathrm{pol}}\frac{p}{mv}. Independence implies

Var⁡(∑BF⁡(xB))≲m−1​𝔼​∑BF⁡(xB).\operatorname{Var}\Big(\sum_{B}F(x_{B})\Big)\lesssim m^{-1}\mathbb{E}\sum_{B}F(x_{B}).

The ratio of variance to squared expectation tends to zero, since it is at most a polynomial factor times vp\frac{v}{p}, and vv has a positive-power upper bound from the pin Frostman estimate. All forward angular and parent and radial-bin upper bounds hold pointwise for any chosen relevant pin. Thus a realization has the required incidence lower bound and all reverse upper bounds. Fixed residue-class selections and subsequent deletions preserve them, at the permitted polynomial cost. ∎

Lemma 23.1 (Preparing uniform pin parents).

Fix finitely many candidate parent widths DjD_{j} and tube widths ρj\rho_{j}, and fix a positive integer LregL_{\mathrm{reg}}, with ϵ=1Lreg\epsilon=\frac{1}{L_{\mathrm{reg}}}. Before the source thinning and the construction of rows, the finite pin set can be restricted at inverse-polynomial cost so that the following hold for every candidate jj:

  1. 1.

    distinct occupied DjD_{j}-parents are at distance at least DjD_{j}.

  2. 2.

    the numbers of retained fine pins in occupied cells are exactly constant at every scale in {Djϵ,Dj2​ϵ,…,Dj,ρj}\{D_{j}^{\epsilon},D_{j}^{2\epsilon},\ldots,D_{j},\rho_{j}\}.

  3. 3.

    after choosing one actual pin independently and uniformly in each occupied ρj\rho_{j}-cell, the numbers of selected pins in occupied cells are exactly constant at the displayed coarser scales.

The finite mass bounds and both angular bounds persist with adjusted polynomial constants. The resulting marked incidence count and pin cardinality satisfy the original lower bounds with adjusted polynomial losses. Consequently the row construction and its richness conclusions can be performed on this already restricted pin set.

Proof.

First retain a dyadic class of marked pin degrees carrying at least an inverse-polynomial fraction of the marked incidences. The degrees are then within a factor two, and the class contains an inverse-polynomial fraction of υf−1\upsilon_{f}^{-1} pins: each degree is at most Cm\frac{C}{m}, while the initial incidence count is at least an inverse-polynomial multiple of (m​υf)−1(m\upsilon_{f})^{-1}. Any subsequent inverse-polynomial fraction of this class preserves an inverse-polynomial fraction of its incidences.

At each candidate DjD_{j}, retain one of the nine residue classes of parent indices modulo three. This loses only a fixed factor at each of finitely many scales and ensures the asserted separation. Apply the usual branching regularization to the finite ancestor tree at the union of the displayed levels. Working from the finest frozen level towards the root, pigeonhole the number of occupied children into dyadic ranges and retain a range carrying an inverse-polynomial fraction of the surviving leaves. The already regularized descendant subtrees have equal size, so this weighted pigeonhole preserves that fraction of fine pins. There are O⁡(n)O(n) possible ranges. Prune each surviving parent to exactly the same power-of-two number of children, and continue recursively. This loses at most an inverse polynomial in nn and leaves an exactly uniform tree at every frozen level. In particular every ρj\rho_{j}-cell has the same number LjL_{j} of fine pins, and every coarser frozen parent has the same number of occupied ρj\rho_{j}-cells. The latter count is unchanged by selecting the actual representative within each cell.

Every retained fine pin has original fine-cell mass at least υf\upsilon_{f}, and every occupied ρj\rho_{j}-cell has original mass in [υj,2​υj)[\upsilon_{j},2\upsilon_{j}). Thus

Lj≲υjυf.L_{j}\lesssim\frac{\upsilon_{j}}{\upsilon_{f}}.

Conversely, there are at most υj−1\upsilon_{j}^{-1} occupied ρj\rho_{j}-cells, whereas the number of surviving fine pins is ≳polυf−1\gtrsim_{\rm pol}\upsilon_{f}^{-1}. Therefore Lj≍polυjυfL_{j}\asymp_{\rm pol}\frac{\upsilon_{j}}{\upsilon_{f}}. The random representatives consequently have the same inclusion probability, to polynomial factors, as in the original pin-coarsening lemma. Its lower-tail argument preserves all rich-pair witness counts and an inverse-polynomial fraction of the generating pins. The reverse angular upper-tail argument is valid in the same experiment. Its expectation is the fine angular count divided by LjL_{j}. All mass bounds refer to the original measure and survive restriction. The forward angular and source-parent estimates hold pointwise, and reverse angular counts can only decrease before the random selection. This proves all claims. Each candidate parent side is replaced by a comparable dyadic side whose logarithmic exponent is divisible by LregL_{\mathrm{reg}}. The comparison factor depends only on LregL_{\mathrm{reg}}. Its logarithmic error is O⁡(Lregn)O(\frac{L_{\mathrm{reg}}}{n}), and the displayed LregL_{\mathrm{reg}}-th roots are then dyadic. This is absorbed in the already selectable scale tolerances. ∎

23.1 A linear dependence on coarse tube occupancy

Lemma 23.2 (Quantitative coarse occupancy).

26   Uniform finite-precision estimates and selection

The lower-box proof uses a new pair at each terminal precision. We therefore need uniform estimates for such changing pairs. This section supplies that uniformity, together with the selection and covering arguments; an asymptotic statement for one fixed pair would not suffice.

Lemma 26.1 (Limits of finite generic pairs).

Fix an oracle AA, 1<σ≤21<\sigma\leq 2, C>0C>0, and a bounded region. Suppose nj→∞n_{j}\to\infty and pairs xj,yjx_{j},y_{j} in that region have |xj−yj|≥nj−C|x_{j}-y_{j}|\geq n_{j}^{-C}. For each n=njn=n_{j}, write x=xj,y=yjx=x_{j},y=y_{j}, e=y−x|y−x|e=\frac{y-x}{|y-x|}, and suppose for every 1≤m≤2​n1\leq m\leq 2n that

KmA​(x),KmA​(y)\displaystyle K_{m}^{A}(x),K_{m}^{A}(y) ≥σ​m−C​log2⁡(n+2),\displaystyle\geq\sigma m-C\log_{2}(n+2), (26.1)
KmA,x​(e),KmA,y​(e)\displaystyle K_{m}^{A,x}(e),K_{m}^{A,y}(e) ≥m−C​log2⁡(n+2),\displaystyle\geq m-C\log_{2}(n+2), (26.2)
KmA,x​(y)\displaystyle K_{m}^{A,x}(y) ≥KmA​(y)−C​log2⁡(n+2),\displaystyle\geq K_{m}^{A}(y)-C\log_{2}(n+2), (26.3)
KmA,y​(x)\displaystyle K_{m}^{A,y}(x) ≥KmA​(x)−C​log2⁡(n+2).\displaystyle\geq K_{m}^{A}(x)-C\log_{2}(n+2). (26.4)

Every joint subsequential limit of the normalized endpoint and conditioned distance profiles satisfies (10.1) in both orientations, with f⁡(u),g⁡(u)≥σ​uf(u),g(u)\geq\sigma u. The conditional-parent transfer of Lemma 14.1 also holds in the finite approximation, with arbitrarily small fixed linear error.

26.1 Uniform estimates for changing pairs

Proof of Lemma 26.1.

We first explain precisely why the retained information estimates survive when (x,y)(x,y) varies with nn. Set

ℓn=⌈(log2⁡(n+2))2⌉,kn=⌈n14⌉,hn=⌈n⌉,\ell_{n}=\lceil(\log_{2}(n+2))^{2}\rceil,\qquad k_{n}=\lceil n^{\frac{1}{4}}\rceil,\qquad h_{n}=\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil,

and fix 1<d<min⁡{σ,54}1<d<\min\{\sigma,\frac{5}{4}\}. For all large nn,

KmA​(x),KmA​(y)≥d​m(ℓn≤m≤2​n).K_{m}^{A}(x),K_{m}^{A}(y)\geq dm\qquad(\ell_{n}\leq m\leq 2n). (26.5)

Thus the point-dependent initial cutoff supplied by effective dimension is replaced by an explicit logarithmic-squared cutoff. On a local projection piece with right endpoint b≥knb\geq k_{n}, a deficiency C​log⁡(n+2)C\log(n+2) is at most 5​C​log⁡(b+2)5C\log(b+2) for all large nn.

The local projection estimates of Stull [33, Lemmas 14–15] are finite statements. Their tolerances, a logarithmic directional deficiency, and a bound on the norm of the point control the threshold. The remark following Lemma 14 states this uniformity explicitly, and the proof of Lemma 15 has the same dependence. Their oracle simulations are uniform. In particular, no threshold depending on an unrecorded property of the selected direction is used here.

For the closed projection estimate, the proof of Lemma 3.2 retains

KRA​(x∣pv​x,v)≤max⁡{KRA​(x)−R,KRA​(x)−u2}+o⁡(n)K_{R}^{A}(x\mid p_{v}x,v)\leq\max\{K_{R}^{A}(x)-R,\frac{K_{R}^{A}(x)-u}{2}\}+o(n) (26.6)

when RR is a fixed positive fraction of nn and uR\frac{u}{R} is bounded below. In fact, for fixed c0,τ,ξ>0c_{0},\tau,\xi>0, the error is at most ξ​R\xi R uniformly for c0​hn≤R≤nc_{0}h_{n}\leq R\leq n and τ​R≤u≤R\tau R\leq u\leq R, once nn is large enough. Its partition has a bounded number of pieces once τ\tau is fixed. Discard projection pieces below knk_{n}, at cost O⁡(kn)=o⁡(R)O(k_{n})=o(R) uniformly in this range. Every remaining piece has a common directional-deficiency constant, and kn≫ℓnk_{n}\gg\ell_{n} ensures that (26.5) supplies the lower dimension cutoff throughout the remaining argument. Sum the bounded number of local estimates with a fixed sufficiently small tolerance. This proves the required uniform version of (26.6), including the smaller projection precisions used inside the prefix partition.

The circle geometry has a second possible dependence on the pair. If |x−z|=|x−y||x-z|=|x-y| and v=y−z|y−z|v=\frac{y-z}{|y-z|}, then

|e⋅v|=|y−z|2​|x−y|.\left|e\cdot v\right|=\frac{|y-z|}{2|x-y|}. (26.7)

Since |x−y|≥n−C|x-y|\geq n^{-C}, approximating vv by a perpendicular to ee loses at most OC​(log⁡n)O_{C}(\log n) bits of precision. The normalization of y−zy-z and the perpendicular-bisector formula have the same uniform logarithmic costs on bounded sets. The tangent transition also widens by only OC​(log⁡n)O_{C}(\log n). The distance-transfer search and the complexity-lowering oracle in Fiedler–Stull [7, Lemmas 14–15] are uniform finite algorithms; their parameter descriptions cost OC​(log⁡n)O_{C}(\log n) here. Supplying a bounded number of additional precision indices does not introduce a point-dependent constant.

These observations account for the pair-dependent quantities, namely the initial lower-complexity cutoff, the directional deficiency, the separation of the endpoints, and the finite parameter descriptions. We next carry out the limit argument using these bounds.

27   Selecting generic pairs at a fixed precision

After a fixed similarity, assume E⊂[0,1]2E\subset[0,1]^{2}. Fix an oracle AA which computes the dyadic masses of μ\mu and finite rational Hausdorff approximations to EE. It is fixed before any bad set or pair is selected.

Lemma 27.1.

Assume the Frostman upper bound μ⁡(B⁡(z,r))≤C​rs\mu(B(z,r))\leq Cr^{s}, s>1s>1, and fix M>0M>0 and 1<σ<s1<\sigma<s. In the other direction, a bounded descendant index selects a center within 2−m2^{-m} of the point.

1<p<min⁡{2−b,b2−a},τ=1−1p>0.1<p<\min\{2-b,\frac{b}{2-a}\},\qquad\tau=1-\frac{1}{p}>0.

The sum of the description and angular exceptional measures is then smaller than (27.5). A remaining pair belongs to B×BB\times B and has all the required finite-precision properties. Since h≳n−Jh\gtrsim n^{-J}, increasing the fixed constant CC also gives |x−y|≥n−C|x-y|\geq n^{-C}. This proves Lemma 27.1.

Remark 27.2.

Neither BB nor its restricted measures are added to the oracle. The mass code always uses the original μ\mu. This avoids a possible circularity between choosing a bad set and selecting incompressible points from it. Shmerkin’s lower box argument [30, Section 6.3] uses the same broad strategy of selecting a pair from a set of mass at least a negative power of the precision. The grid and Kraft estimates above give the version needed for the present complexity hypotheses.

27.4 Coding a small pinned cover

Lemma 27.3.

For the fixed oracle AA above, there is a constant cc such that for every x∈Ex\in E, r∈Δx​Er\in\Delta_{x}E, and n≥1n\geq 1,

KnA,x​(r)≤log2⁡N2−n​(Δx​E)+c​log2⁡(n+2).K_{n}^{A,x}(r)\leq\log_{2}N_{2^{-n}}(\Delta_{x}E)+c\log_{2}(n+2). (27.6)
Proof.

Using AA and the oracle xx, compute a finite rational approximation to Δx​E\Delta_{x}E with Hausdorff error at most 2−n100\frac{2^{-n}}{100}. Round its members to a grid of mesh 2−n4\frac{2^{-n}}{4} and remove repetitions. The resulting list is a 2−n2^{-n}-net for Δx​E\Delta_{x}E. It has at most a fixed constant times N2−n​(Δx​E)N_{2^{-n}}(\Delta_{x}E) members, since an interval of radius 2−n2^{-n}, enlarged by the approximation error, meets only a bounded number of the grid cells. The index of a suitable list member, together with nn, has length at most the right side of (27.6). The algorithm is the same for every pin. ∎

The cover bound is an upper bound for the description of every distance at that pin. That is why two bad pins force the common distance to be short in both orientations.

29   The geometric contradiction near the endpoint

The rigid plateau has a concrete geometric meaning. The source parent at exponent 310\frac{3}{10} admits very little mass in any one annulus, while the pin measure is spread over the scales between 15\frac{1}{5} and 35\frac{3}{5}. We show that these two facts are incompatible with only δ−45\delta^{-\frac{4}{5}} radii at each pin. The finite statement below records the hypotheses separately from the one-sided plateau parameters used earlier.

If the support separation is only n−Cn^{-C}, angular rounding and the circle-to-bisector identities introduce fixed powers of nn. 29.1 Realizing the finite hypotheses on a common relation

Fix a Frostman measure, an oracle encoding it and its compact support, a lower dimension exponent greater than one, and a polynomial relation-mass loss n−Mn^{-M}. 0<η0<min⁡{η⁡(ε),ε,340}0<\eta_{0}<\min\left\{\eta(\varepsilon),\varepsilon,\frac{3}{40}\right\}

with any further fixed reduction needed to absorb the errors above.
