30   The universal unpinned and lower-box bounds

30.1 General unpinned Hausdorff dimension

Suppose a compact EE with dimHE>1\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E>1 satisfies dimHΔ​E<45+η0\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta E<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}. Choose qq strictly between these two numbers. Choose a Frostman measure of exponent greater than one and restrict it to separated source and pin portions, denoted by μ\mu and ν\nu. Encode the measure and the compact set using a base oracle AA as in Section 5. The effectively compact point-to-set principle implies

lim infnKnA​(|x−y|)n<q\liminf_{n}\frac{K_{n}^{A}(|x-y|)}{n}<q

for every pair of points in these portions. Work with a slightly smaller intermediate threshold so that logarithmic coding costs can be absorbed in q​nqn.

On the fixed positive-measure good-pair relation GG, both directional hypotheses, full-oracle independence estimates, angular-density restrictions, and base mass codes hold. Let RnR_{n} retain pairs with low unconditioned distance complexity. Each pair belongs to infinitely many such RnR_{n}. The Tonelli argument in Lemma 20.4 gives (ν×μ)​(Rn)≥n−2(\nu\times\mu)(R_{n})\geq n^{-2} at infinitely many scales. Low unconditioned complexity implies low complexity in both orientations:

KnA,x​(|x−y|),KnA,y​(|x−y|)≤q​n+O⁡(log⁡n).K_{n}^{A,x}(|x-y|),\ K_{n}^{A,y}(|x-y|)\leq qn+O(\log n).

Bin the two endpoint profiles and the distance profiles jointly; there are no⁡(1)n^{o(1)} records on the usual slowly growing scale mesh. A common retained relation still has polynomial mass.

The resulting bilateral profiles and common finite configurations are excluded by Section 29, since q<45+η0q<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}. This proves Theorem 1.2 for compact sets. For analytic sets, first choose a compact subset with Hausdorff dimension greater than one; its distance set is contained in the original distance set.

A recurrent relation of low distance complexity need not contain many pairs in a single profile class; a dense relation can connect two different classes. Therefore finite matching alone does not justify the Hausdorff conclusion. Proposition 13.1 removes precisely that restriction. It does not improve the abstract scalar four-fifths bound by itself. The geometric contradiction is still essential.

30.2 Internal pinned lower box dimension

For Bn={x∈E:N2−n​(Δx​E)<2q​n}B_{n}=\{x\in E:N_{2^{-n}}(\Delta_{x}E)<2^{qn}\} we prove

μ⁡(Bn)≤n−M\mu(B_{n})\leq n^{-M}

for every fixed M>0M>0 at all sufficiently large nn, whenever q<45+η0q<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}. We use Lemmas 26.1, 27.1, and 27.3. If this conclusion fails, choose two polynomially separated portions of BnB_{n} and retain a polynomial-mass product relation. Both endpoints are bad pins at the same original precision, so both conditioned distance complexities are low.

Joint binning of arbitrary endpoint profiles suffices, because Proposition 13.1 allows f≠gf\neq g. The finite geometric contradiction above then proves the same quantitative tail bound. Borel–Cantelli proves the almost-everywhere lower-box claim. A Frostman measure on a hypothetical internal exceptional set of dimension greater than one contradicts this conclusion; closure extends that conclusion from compact to arbitrary bounded EE, since lower box dimension is unchanged by closure.

Together with Section 28, this proves Theorem 1.3. For q<L∗​(s)q<L_{*}(s), either q<L⁡(s)q<L(s) or q<45+η0q<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}, so one of the two tail estimates applies. The same exceptional-set argument proves (1.5).

31   The gains and the remaining limitations

The universal unpinned estimate improves 34\frac{3}{4} by 120+η0\frac{1}{20}+\eta_{0}. The gain has two parts. Reciprocal partition estimates account for 120\frac{1}{20}; endpoint rigidity and the common-source geometry account for η0\eta_{0}. The universal external pinned gain is q∗−34=0.03131​…q_{*}-\frac{3}{4}=0.03131\ldots. The distinctions between these arguments matter when considering how far the methods can be pushed.

31.1 What can be improved, and the limits of the methods

There is one proved obstruction to a uniform pinned improvement using only the pointwise inequalities of this paper. Proposition 7.3 constructs abstract profiles satisfying both prefix estimates and both transfer estimates strengthened by the full partition functional, with f⁡(u),g⁡(u)≥(1+θ)​uf(u),g(u)\geq(1+\theta)u but dx​(1)=34+θd_{x}(1)=\frac{3}{4}+\theta and dy​(1)=1d_{y}(1)=1 for every sufficiently small θ>0\theta>0. Consequently, further optimization of those same constraints cannot force a fixed positive improvement over 34\frac{3}{4} at a prescribed pin. The common-source mass bounds supply an additional constraint, and it is this additional information that permits our pinned improvement. The obstruction concerns the stated scalar inequalities. We do not prove that its profiles come from a pair of points satisfying all the geometric hypotheses, or that every possible pointwise argument has the same limitation.

31.2 The scalar obstruction at four fifths

The reciprocal argument reaches 45\frac{4}{5}. The next proposition shows that the scalar inequalities used in that argument cannot force a larger universal constant. In the construction, the excess f⁡(u)−uf(u)-u first rises, stays constant for an interval of length t5\frac{t}{5}, and then falls. A partition piece of length at most t5\frac{t}{5} cannot join any of that rise to the later fall. We use this separation to compute the partition loss directly.

Proposition 31.1 (The terminal-flat profiles).

For 1<t≤541<t\leq\frac{5}{4}, put, on [0,1][0,1],

f⁡(u)=g⁡(u)=min⁡{2​u,u+2​t5,t},dx​(u)=dy​(u)=min⁡{u,4​t5}.f(u)=g(u)=\min\{2u,u+\frac{2t}{5},t\},\qquad d_{x}(u)=d_{y}(u)=\min\{u,\frac{4t}{5}\}.

The functions f,gf,g are nondecreasing and 22-Lipschitz, and dx,dyd_{x},d_{y} are nondecreasing and 11-Lipschitz. All four vanish at zero. These profiles satisfy f⁡(u),g⁡(u)≥t​uf(u),g(u)\geq tu, the ordinary prefix inequalities, and both full transfer inequalities

for 0<a≤b≤10<a\leq b\leq 1. They also satisfy every strengthened prefix

31.3 The two geometric comparisons

The first geometric upper count has a sharper local limitation. For a fixed admissible restricted-sum exponent α\alpha, the comparison in (21.11) is

L−U1≥3​α4​(1−2​Δ)−(10−3​α)​ω.L-U_{1}\geq\frac{3\alpha}{4}(1-2\Delta)-(10-3\alpha)\omega.

The coefficient 10−3​α10-3\alpha is attained in the abstract parameter range of Proposition 21.1 by ς=2\varsigma=2, χ=−1\chi=-1, u0=𝔢=0u_{0}=\mathfrak{e}=0, ϖ=1\varpi=1, and 𝔲=2\mathfrak{u}=2. At transfer level one, where Δ=0\Delta=0 and q=34+ωq=\frac{3}{4}+\omega, this uniform comparison therefore requires

q<34+3​α40−12​α.q<\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3\alpha}{40-12\alpha}.

Letting α↗α∗\alpha\nearrow\alpha_{*} yields q∗q_{*}. Optimizing the same coefficient over the same parameter range cannot improve this bound. It could improve if a stronger restricted-sum estimate supplied a larger admissible α\alpha, if one of the geometric counts improved, or if additional geometric information excluded the parameters attaining the coefficient. We make no claim that those parameters are realized by the configurations arising from a common source measure. Nor do we claim that α∗\alpha_{*} is the optimal restricted-sum exponent. Substituting a stronger input would also require checking the other scale and richness inequalities in the proof.

The second upper count uses angular information from both endpoints. Its effective parent exponent is

Beff=min⁡{ζ,α+(2−3​α)​a},B_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min\{\zeta,\alpha+(2-3\alpha)a\},

and Section 23 compares the lower count with both entries. The resulting sufficient conditions are

ω<−1+4​α+6​(1−2​α)​Δ12​(3−2​α),ω<α⁡(1−2​Δ)4​(2+α).\omega<\frac{-1+4\alpha+6(1-2\alpha)\Delta}{12(3-2\alpha)},\qquad\omega<\frac{\alpha(1-2\Delta)}{4(2+\alpha)}.

After the certificate iteration these become q<Qbq<Q_{b} and q<Qfq<Q_{f}. Their minimum is the bound proved in Section 24. The controlling branch changes at SswitchS_{\mathrm{switch}} after α↗α∗\alpha\nearrow\alpha_{*}. At a fixed source dimension, improving only the larger branch leaves the minimum unchanged. Improving the smaller branch requires a better count, a stronger angular bound, or a further restriction on the allowable row and parent scales. The verified branch switch is exact for the two displayed formulas, but the paper does not prove that these formulas describe the best possible use of the common relation. In particular, the present second comparison does not raise the universal pinned constant as the source dimension decreases to one. Proposition E.1 in Appendix E also shows that combining the two displayed counts before optimizing does not improve their threshold within the stated parameter set. Two explicit choices of parameters suffice to prove this limitation. They need not arise from a common source measure.

The constant continuation Y⁡(t)=78Y(t)=\frac{7}{8} for t≥S0t\geq S_{0} comes from the range Δ<18\Delta<\frac{1}{8} of the reciprocal estimate. In the source-dimension iteration, the limiting value of Δ\Delta reaches 18\frac{1}{8} at t=S0t=S_{0}. The matching-profile argument reaches the same boundary when the source floor is 98\frac{9}{8}. Extending these calculations requires further control at and beyond this transfer level. The value 78\frac{7}{8} is not an upper bound for the other methods of the paper; R⁡(t)R(t) exceeds it for larger tt.

The fixed gain η0\eta_{0} uses a strict geometric exponent gap of 295\frac{2}{95} at the limiting configuration. This number is not the value of η0\eta_{0}. A numerical dimension gain would require quantitative control of the stability lemma and all subsequent tolerances. The qualitative argument suffices for the stated theorem.

Several losses affect the scale at which a contradiction occurs but not its limiting exponent. Fixed multiplicative constants, dyadic rounding, and polynomial factors in nn change the logarithms of the counts by at most O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n). Coding errors have the same order. These contributions vanish after division by nn. The fixed exponent tolerances are chosen arbitrarily small after a positive leading margin has been established. Removing these losses alone cannot turn a zero leading margin into a positive one or raise the constants above. Likewise, the exceptional-set threshold one uses radial projection input with source and pin exponents greater than one. Extending that part of the proof to smaller pin exponents needs an appropriate replacement for that input, not only a numerical reoptimization of the final count.

Finally, every distance set is a subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}, so its Hausdorff dimension is at most one. The conclusions giving full pinned dimension when dimHE≥32\dim_{\mathrm{H}}E\geq\frac{3}{2} have already reached this absolute ceiling. Below that range, the paper proves the obstructions and limits of individual comparisons described above. It does not determine the best bound obtainable by combining all the information in a common-source configuration. The optimal unpinned constant and the optimal use of the two pinned geometric counts remain open.

Question 31.2.

Question 31.3.

Can the two-sided angular information in the common relation raise the universal pinned constant q∗q_{*}, rather than only the bound at larger source dimensions?

Question 31.4.

What additional compatibility across scales would turn the finite rich-bisector counts into a Hausdorff-dimension estimate for one fixed limiting family of rich bisectors?

Appendix C An elementary iteration of the scalar bounds

The first argument used only a lower bound on the tail of each profile. The interval estimates also give information at intermediate scales. We use that information twice, and then return to the tail. This produces an affine update for the cutoff from which the full tail transfers. Its fixed point determines the exponent 27253521\frac{2725}{3521}.

The calculation below shows how iterating the cutoff improves the initial bound. The reciprocal argument in Section 10 develops this idea further.

Remark C.2 (Finiteness and the role of the transfer lemma).

For every fixed q<27253521q<\frac{2725}{3521}, only finitely many updates are needed. Within each update all interval endpoints are fixed positive proportions of the terminal precision, and Lemma 4.1 holds for every such pair of endpoints. The proof does not sum a precision-dependent number of error terms. Proposition C.1 improves the scalar consequence of the same analytic inputs. Its conversion to the distance-set statement uses the same fixed-pair and classical arguments as the 1317\frac{13}{17} bound.

Appendix D Pinned consequences of matching profiles

Finite-scale matching allowed us to choose a different pair at each precision in the lower-box argument. A common dyadic mass law ensures matching for almost every fixed pair. We can then use the same scalar estimates to obtain a pinned Hausdorff bound. The geometric argument supplies the fixed gain near dimension one.

Proposition D.1 (A matched-profile pinned consequence).

Suppose x≠yx\neq y satisfy (H1)–(H4) relative to AA, and

sup1≤m≤r|KmA​(x)−KmA​(y)|=o⁡(r).\sup_{1\leq m\leq r}|K_{m}^{A}(x)-K_{m}^{A}(y)|=o(r). (D.1)

If dimAx,dimAy>1+κ\dim^{A}x,\dim^{A}y>1+\kappa with 0<κ<180<\kappa<\frac{1}{8}, then

lim infr→∞KrA,x​(|x−y|)r≥45+3​κ5.\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{K_{r}^{A,x}(|x-y|)}{r}\geq\frac{4}{5}+\frac{3\kappa}{5}.
Proof.

Take any sequence of terminal precisions and extract uniformly convergent endpoint profiles and the distance profile dxd_{x}. Condition (D.1) implies f=gf=g. The prefix and both transfer expressions therefore agree in the two orientations. Hence (f,f,dx,dx)(f,f,d_{x},d_{x}) is a scalar system, with f⁡(u)≥(1+κ)​uf(u)\geq(1+\kappa)u. Proposition 12.1 proves the lower bound at the terminal scale. The initial sequence was arbitrary, which proves the assertion. The two actual conditioned distance profiles need not agree. ∎

Theorem D.2 (Pinned distances under a common dyadic mass law).

Let μ\mu be a compactly supported planar ss-Frostman probability measure, with s>1s>1, and put E=supp⁡μE=\operatorname{supp}\mu. Suppose there are real numbers H⁡(n)H(n) such that

−log2⁡μ⁡(Qn​(z))=H⁡(n)+oz​(n)for μ-almost every ​z.-\log_{2}\mu(Q_{n}(z))=H(n)+o_{z}(n)\quad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }z.

Then dimHΔx​E≥L∗​(s)\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq L_{*}(s) for μ\mu-almost every xx. The quotient H⁡(n)n\frac{H(n)}{n} need not converge.

The mass law says that the linear-scale part of the information in a dyadic cell is described by one function H⁡(n)H(n) at almost every point. It permits the rate of information growth to vary with the scale.

Proof.

Choose an oracle AA encoding EE and all dyadic masses of μ\mu. Lemma 2.2 implies KnA​(z)=H⁡(n)+oz​(n)K_{n}^{A}(z)=H(n)+o_{z}(n) almost everywhere. For almost every pair, the difference of the two complexities is o⁡(n)o(n). This implies (D.1) as well. Given a positive tolerance, the errors at all sufficiently large m≤rm\leq r are at most that tolerance times rr; the finitely many smaller errors are bounded independently of rr.

The same coding lemma with the other endpoint as an additional oracle, followed by Fubini, proves full-oracle independence for almost every pair. The Frostman bound ensures effective dimension at least ss. To obtain the directional hypotheses, fix 1<s′<s1<s^{\prime}<s and apply Orponen’s theorem [25, Theorem 1.11] to countably many source restrictions in balls separated from the pin. The exceptional centers have dimension at most 2−s′<12-s^{\prime}<1 and are μ\mu-null. Directions failing the logarithmic complexity bound form an arclength-null set. Absolute continuity and Fubini therefore supply both directional estimates.

For almost every xx, Proposition D.1 applies to almost every yy, for each 0<κ<min⁡{s−1,18}0<\kappa<\min\{s-1,\frac{1}{8}\}. Letting κ\kappa increase to this upper endpoint proves dimA,x|x−y|≥L⁡(s)\dim^{A,x}|x-y|\geq L(s). The pinned image is effectively compact relative to (A,x)(A,x), so the effectively compact point-to-set principle proves the Hausdorff bound L⁡(s)L(s).

It remains to prove the fixed gain. Suppose a positive measure set of pins has pinned Hausdorff dimension below some q<45+η0q<\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}. By a countable restriction, choose separated source and pin portions of positive measure. The common mass law and the preceding generic properties can be made uniform on a positive product-measure relation. Restrictions to positive-measure sets preserve the law, since the dyadic density theorem makes their cell-mass ratio tend to a positive constant at almost every retained point.

Lemma 20.4 supplies infinitely many precisions with a relation of polynomial mass and low conditioned distance complexity in the prescribed orientation. The endpoint profiles agree uniformly in the limit. The distance profile in that orientation can therefore be duplicated to form (f,f,dx,dx)(f,f,d_{x},d_{x}). Lemma 13.3 now forces the plateau and parent certificate used in Proposition 29.1. That proposition needs the small radial cover in only the actual prescribed orientation. The duplicated scalar profile is used solely to obtain its mass and plateau hypotheses. Its contradiction proves the bound 45+η0\frac{4}{5}+\eta_{0}. Taking the maximum with L⁡(s)L(s) completes the proof. ∎

Corollary D.3 (Uniform branching).

Start with a dyadic square. At level nn, retain mn∈{1,2,3,4}m_{n}\in\{1,2,3,4\} children of every retained square, using the same number for all parents at that level. Their locations may vary with the parent. Let EE be the limiting compact set and let μ\mu give equal mass to the retained cells. If

s0=lim infn→∞1n​log⁡∏k=1n2⁡mk>1,s_{0}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}\prod_{k=1}^{n}m_{k}>1,

then dimHΔx​E≥L∗​(s0)\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\Delta_{x}E\geq L_{*}(s_{0}) for μ\mu-almost every xx.

Proof.

Put H⁡(n)=∑k=1nlog2⁡mkH(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log_{2}m_{k}. Each retained cell has mass 2−H⁡(n)2^{-H(n)}. Dyadic boundary lines are null. A bounded vertical or horizontal segment meets at most C​2nC2^{n} cells, whose total mass is at most C​2n−H⁡(n)→0C2^{n-H(n)}\to 0. A ball of radius 2−n2^{-n} meets a bounded number of cells, so μ\mu is tt-Frostman for some t>1t>1. Apply the preceding theorem at every Frostman exponent below s0s_{0} and use continuity of L∗L_{*}. The dyadic mass identity is exact. ∎

Alternating two-child and four-child blocks of lengths 2j2^{j}, j≥1j\geq 1, gives lim infn→∞H⁡(n)n=43\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(n)}{n}=\frac{4}{3} and lim supn→∞H⁡(n)n=53\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(n)}{n}=\frac{5}{3}. The ratio is monotone within each block. This illustrates why the hypothesis concerns an entire information profile rather than a single limit of the information per scale. For the Hausdorff conclusion, the common law supplies one fixed pair along all sequences of precisions. The lower-box proof needed only the finite-scale matching of Section 28.

All these thresholds lie in the stated structural range whenever they control the maximum, since α<α∗<25\alpha<\alpha_{*}<\frac{2}{5} implies ωf<1−2​Δ24\omega_{f}<\frac{1-2\Delta}{24}. All the displayed template constraints, including 3​ς+2​χ≤43\varsigma+2\chi\leq 4, ς≥max⁡{0,−2​χ}\varsigma\geq\max\{0,-2\chi\}, and 0≤𝔢≤ς0\leq\mathfrak{e}\leq\varsigma, hold for the two choices. For both choices one may take u−=Wu_{-}=W and u+=W+tu_{+}=W+t, so the remaining plateau-location inequalities hold as well. This completes the calculation. ∎
